#3276. Every Track From ‘Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album’ Ranked — Now Including the Deluxe Bonus Tracks

GTA's accompanying soundtrack arrived 24 hours after the long-anticipated Rockstar video game — and they didn't waste time releasing the deluxe edition days later.

Monocultural moments in society have become extremely rare in the mid-2020s, but the arrival of Grand Theft Auto VI has brought about as strong a unified pop-culture tidal wave as we’ve seen this decade.

Rockstar Games released the Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album on Friday (Nov. 20) through Atlantic Records as an accompanying soundtrack to the long-awaited video game, which arrived 24 hours earlier.

As Billboard details in our latest cover story about the songs, score and soundtrack of GTA VI, Rockstar didn’t spare any expense when plotting the music for the immersive game. The original 34-song soundtrack features Playboi Carti, Dua Lipa, Cardi B, Lana Del Rey, Gunna, Don Toliver, Kodak Black, Yung Lean, Future, Metro Boomin, Travis Scott, Fred again.., PinkPantheress, Morgan Wallen, Tame Impala, Fuerza Regida and more.

GTA VI will look to make even more history with a No. 1 debut on the charts — as no video game soundtrack has topped the Billboard 200 before.

Artist-hosted radio stations dominate the Vice City airwaves, with stations helmed or curated by the likes of Bad Bunny, Lana Del Rey, Morgan Wallen, Trina and Trick Daddy, PinkPantheress, Burna Boy and Robyn.

The Grand Theft Auto VI festivities will continue into the weekend, with a music festival at Miami’s Mana Wynwood on Nov. 21. The festival is set to have Cardi B, Travis Scott, Rauw Alejandro and more hit the stage, including a Cactus Jack ensemble featuring Scott, Don Toliver, SoFaygo and a cameo from Florida’s own Kodak Black.

After GTA hit pop culture with a tsunami takeover, Rockstar Games and Atlantic Records continued to flood the marketplace with a 23-track deluxe edition of the album, which arrived on Monday (Nov. 23). They didn’t stop there, as an iTunes exclusive four-pack was released on Tuesday (Nov. 24) to ensure the full-court press.

Take a break from perusing Leonida with Jason and Lucia and find all of the tracks from the Grand Theft Auto: The Album along with the new deluxe edition (sans the five Overmono songs that feel more like a score) and iTunes exclusives ranked in order below.

Who knew Omar Apollo had a funky little party-starter like this up his sleeve? Drawing on the iconic Stalag riddim immortalized by Sister Nancy’s “Bam Bam,” “No Me Busques” bursts with a wailing chorus with an infectious call-and-response hook. Oh, and that festive saxophone riff. Lyrically, there’s not much to it beyond Apollo’s repeated insistence that someone stop looking for him. The groove does most of the talking. — ISABELA RAYGOZA

This track is a little different from what I’m used to, but I like it. It plays during the opening credits of GTA VI and serves as the opening track on the game’s album. Sonically, it has a heavy ’80s-inspired synth pulse, electro-disco drums and electric piano that make me feel like it could fit perfectly into any season of Stranger Things.

It’s the perfect way to open the game’s soundtrack. The song is about starting from zero and hustling your way toward success, which feels right at home in the world of GTA. It sets the tone for the kind of journey players are about to embark on. — CHRISTOPHER CLAXTON

Joe Armon-Jones is here to lower your cortisol levels while strolling around Leonida, listening to the luscious instrumentation of “Hotel Alphonso.” — M.S.

Sak pase? Kodak Black teams up with DJ Michael Brun and the duo connects with their Haitian roots, as Yak mixes in Haitian Creole while playfully roasting someone’s baldy haircut and rapping about flipping cocaine. — M.S.

GTA is supposed to have something for everyone, and the metalheads make their presence felt with the thrash aggression of Power Trip’s “Mutual Death Warrant.” I’m ready to either run through a wall or fire up Guitar Hero after pressing play thanks to the Dallas band. — M.S.

The Dare’s synth-heavy brand of dance-punk has invaded the mainstream thanks to pop stars like Charli xcx and ADÉLA leaning into and elevating the subgenre. He serves up the robotic “Interesting” here, which will spin on the EDM radio stations around Leonida and get The Dare a set at Space replica The Vault in Vice City. — M.S.

Separate from his nu-disco Holy Ghost! running mate Nick Millhiser, Alex Frankel wants you to dance in Leonida with the groovy “Playa Rosa,” which is perfect for a top-down cruise down the coastline or a night at The Vault. — M.S.

This is an interesting track and an unapologetically raunchy celebration of sexual confidence, which is exactly the kind of energy we can expect from Sexyy Red. Real Dimez and Sexyy lean into their provocative personalities for a playful record that doesn’t take itself too seriously. Even the title “Cooties” plays on the childhood idea that girls have cooties and that boys stay away from them because they’re afraid of infection. Now, the tables have turned and these ladies are having fun with the concept. — C.C.

A dance-house track that makes it clear this duo doesn’t play around — and that anyone can catch a beatdown. — C.C.

Primal percussion, glitchy electronics and unbridled sexual energy collide on Arca’s self-produced “Sandunguea.” The Venezuelan experimentalist delivers a delirious invitation to dance and indulge, peppering her verses with colorful slang from her homeland. Against abrasive beats, her vocals switch between flirtation and feverish demands, breathy moans and fragmented chants. “Nuestra pasarela es la calle” (the street is our runway), she declares. In true Arca fashion, the dance floor becomes a space for uninhibited self-expression, where pleasure and chaos go hand in hand. — I.R.

“All Again” is about missing someone after a relationship has ended, and wondering whether the love, memories and heartbreak were worth it in the end. It captures that feeling of looking back on a relationship and questioning whether you’d put yourself through it all over again. I’m not sure I would. Would you? — C.C.

After closing out Grand Theft Auto V with the final credits track “The Setup,” Favored Nations returns to push the tempo on the sixth installment’s iTunes-exclusive foursome with the blissful “There Is Only Us.” — M.S.

Rina Sawayama made waves with her assist on Charli xcx’s “Beg for You” in 2022, and the Japanese pop artist/model is back in the mainstream with the brooding “TRDWFE.” I’m going to be hearing Sawayama asking us to “submit” repeatedly when my head hits the pillow tonight — although “TRDWFE” sounds like it was tailor-made more for the likes of HBO’s The Idol than the GTA vibe. — MICHAEL SAPONARA

With Travis Scott all over Grand Theft Auto‘s rollout, it’s only right he reserved a slot for one of Cactus Jack’s offspring. Sofaygo makes the most of his appearance on “Cashout,” a syrupy melodic blend that SahBabii would’ve been a perfect running mate for. — M.S.

It’s clear that 21 Savage will stand ten toes down on his reputation, street credibility and distrust of his opps. Throughout the track, he draws a line between people who talk about violence and those who are actually willing to stand on business. Savage doesn’t want listeners to forget that actions speak louder than words, and if you’re not really about it, he has no time to waste on you. Don’t forget, Twitter fingers will get you nowhere. As he puts it, “We get up and go at all the smoke, you n—as go live.” — C.C.

Metro is back on production for this one. It’s a quick track about flexing, so you already know the deal: money, cars, clothes and relationships. Thug keeps it short and straight to the point, delivering the kind of flex-heavy record that fits right into the GTA lifestyle. Just remember, anything born out of a criminal lifestyle comes with real consequences. — C.C.

“You Move Me” was made for a top-down cruise through Leonida. NEIL FRANCES’ blend of disco and EDM gives a callback to 1980s Vice City, but something that still feels like it could exist in the modern dance world. — M.S.

Young Nudy lives at the intersection of gaming and rap, so Nudy making an appearance on the soundtrack shouldn’t come as much of a surprise. He serves up the sinister “Don Da Da,” which finds him as a kingpin calling shots, while the track could’ve been an offshoot that didn’t make the cut from his Just Doin Me project. — M.S.

Fcukers is back. The NYC duo’s first release since Ö comes with the house-leaning “Only One” and they’re here to start the party and blow out your speakers. If there’s a rave somewhere in Leonida, Fcukers is headlining. Can we get Tinashe to sprinkle her Popstar magic on a remix? Vocalist Shanny Wise even moonlights as a co-host of GTA Radio’s Stockyard FM alongside PinkPantheress and The Dare in the video game. — M.S.

All the baddies to the front, please! “GMA” stands for “Get Money Anthem,” because if you can’t make money in GTA, what the hell can you do? Hope y’all caught that reference. This is an upbeat party anthem celebrating women who make their own money, no matter how they earn it. JT isn’t knocking anybody’s hustle, and at this point, neither am I. Whether you’re stacking cash in the game or in real life, the message is to stay focused on your goals and tune out the criticism. Shoutout to all the ladies working traditional 9-to-5s, earning college degrees, dancing or hustling on the side. We see you! — C.C.

Keith Richards puts his own spin on Jimmy Reed’s 1961 blues classic “Bright Lights, Big City” for Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album. His version takes a different approach from Reed’s original, but Keith sounds right at home here. It’s a fresh take on a blues classic, and one that fits perfectly into the world of GTA. — C.C.

Fame is a hell of a drug, but Denzel Curry and 454 haven’t forgotten where they came from. “FLA Flow” is a tribute to Florida’s music and hip-hop culture, with both artists reflecting on the street history and neighborhoods that shaped them. — C.C.

The crown jewel of the iTunes exclusive four-pack. 100 gecs wax poetic about their love for marijuana and affinity for getting high on the punk-leaning smoker’s delight “Sensimilla,” while also making time to take shots at Tiger King star Carole Baskin.

With GTA returning to Vice City, having Kodak Black involved was a must. He’s even a character playing himself in the video game’s campaign. A Yak and Don Toliver collaboration seems like an odd pairing on its face — then you mix in the chaotic skittering production, and both the artists and listeners are playing catch-up for the duration of “Let’s Rock.” — M.S.

Opium’s HXG and Tana invite Quavo to their rage rap world with “RCKSTRL!VING” and Huncho makes it work with his trap-laden rhymes mixing in with the grungy soundscape. The rapper-rockstar lifestyle plays an integral role in GTA VI‘s chapter three when the scene switches to downtown Vice City. — M.S.

Offset will always be unapologetic, and “I Just Came To Pop It” is no different. Wealth, status, street credibility and a refusal to back down from anyone are all on display. Offset brags about the lifestyle he’s built, from luxury cars to expensive jewelry, while reflecting on his past in the trap and the life he gets to live today. The contrast between his street beginnings and his multimillion-dollar lifestyle is a reminder of just how far he’s come. You earned it, so pop your s—t, Offset! — C.C.

Tee Grizzley is not one to mess with. “IKYFL” is an unapologetic statement about loyalty, street credibility, success and refusing to let anyone question how far he’s come. The track captures Tee’s mentality of protecting his circle, enjoying the rewards of his success and staying ready for anyone who tries to challenge him. This is one of those tracks that makes you feel untouchable when you’re cruising through Vice City. — C.C.

“Got Dat” debuted on Vice City Rap Radio in GTA VI, and lands on streaming services with the album’s deluxe. Pooh Shiesty’s menacing trap-laden rhymes are a perfect fit for GTA, but, unfortunately, Pooh living out that outlaw lifestyle has landed him behind bars for the foreseeable future. — M.S.

Morgan Wallen colors outside the lines of country while leaning on his pop and R&B influences for “Last Thing You Need.” It’s a smooth, laid-back track for fans to throw on for a late-night cruise through the swamp lands of GTA‘s Leonida. — M.S.

Just when you think you’ve settled into the sleek reggaetón groove of “X,” JHAYCO throws a dance-floor curveball. Co-produced by the Puerto Rican star alongside Tainy and COZY, the track finds Jhay assuring a love interest that he’s nothing like her ex, dishing out a stream of suggestive compliments. But the real thrill comes during the bridge, when bright synths and a pulsating electronic beat give way to a euphoric break before the dembow kicks back in. It’s a catchy little club banger that doubles as a reminder of Jhay’s knack for melding reggaetón with EDM. — I.R.

Of course, the GTA team got the legend Robert Glasper to help close out the album! Bringing together bassist Stanley Clarke, drummer Yussef Dayes and pianist Robert Glasper, this track is straight vibes. No lyrics needed, just let the musicians do their thing. Named after Miami’s historic Overtown neighborhood, the track connects the game’s Vice City map to the real-world roots of Miami. A smooth way to bring the album home. — C.C.

Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album wouldn’t be complete without an Afro-fusion track like this. I love the simple, chant-like hook. This might become my new go-to morning affirmation before heading to work or starting a session in GTA. It’s an uplifting song about resilience, bouncing back from setbacks and continuing to reach for greater heights no matter who or what tries to hold you back.

This is the perfect song to play after a mission doesn’t go as planned. Burna is reminding us that no matter the setback or how people treat you, you’re still unstoppable. Nobody is better than you, so keep pushing and get “bigger, bigger, bigger, bigger, hey!” — C.C.

This is baby-making music. Dâm-Funk and The Time’s Jesse Johnson supply the groovy, funky vibes that have been a staple of the GTA series for over two decades. I’m glad the soundtrack composers made room for them here, because Gen Z isn’t going to know what hit them when a new generation of gamers presses play. — M.S.

Grief, trauma and the emotional exhaustion of being unable to escape memories of someone you’ve lost are at the center of HEALTH’s “NIGHTMARE.” The song uses the idea of a nightmare as a metaphor for being trapped in an endless cycle of emotional pain, where the past continues to haunt you. However, by the second half of the track, HEALTH begins shifting toward the idea of waking up, moving forward and learning to separate the past from the present. — C.C.

Tove Lo wasn’t a name I expected to see on the tracklist for GTA VI, but she makes it work and shuts down any detractors who didn’t think she’d belong. “Blood in Your Eyes” is the blaring experimental pop that should be pumping the dance floor at Leonida’s version of the Space and E11EVEN nightclubs in the game. — M.S.

JENNIE is taking another “Power Trip” with this dance-pop track. In JENNIE’s city, there are no limits. This is a celebration of confidence, status and the freedom to do whatever you want without worrying about who approves. She embraces a larger-than-life persona, putting herself at the center of attention while making it clear that she knows her worth. But there’s nothing wrong with a little self-love, so is this really a power trip? — C.C.

If you see Future and Metro Boomin on a track, nine times out of 10, it’s going to be a banger, and this song proves just that. Shoutout to Yung Lean, because I like the track, but I’m not entirely sure if his presence fits. We have Metro handling the production, of course, and Future’s trap-influenced sound just works perfectly over Metro’s production. The two have such a natural chemistry, and this track is another example of why their collaborations rarely miss.– C.C.

Zara Larsson is chasing carefree desire with “Fast Emotion,” and she has no shame about it. She just wants you to “make it reckless, leave [her] breathless, make [her] heart race.” This track is bright, upbeat and full of energy, making it perfect for cruising down Vice City. “Fast Emotion” is all about craving an intense, spontaneous connection and allowing yourself to get swept up in the excitement of the moment. Through imagery of summer nights, physical attraction and speed, Zara captures a romance that feels exhilarating. — C.C.

Outside of Drake, no rapper made more of 2026 than Don Toliver. “TF?” provides the gloomy soundscape where Toliver is at home, compared to “Let’s Rock.” The raunchy tune could’ve been left on the cutting room floor during his OCTANE sessions, but is a worthy addition to the GTA album. — M.S.

A Cherokee loaded with contraband, police sirens blaring and a desperate escape through the city — “Macacoa 2000” opens like a scene straight out of Grand Theft Auto. Over hard-hitting reggaetón produced by Dímelo Ninow, reminiscent of the genre’s gritty 2000s heyday, Rauw Alejandro narrates a chaotic cop chase in a rapid-fire flow. Near the end, the track switches gears into sultrier territory, with the silky R&B vocals that marked his breakthrough. But beneath the bravado is a deeper reverence for reggaetón’s roots. At the beginning, he salutes the genre’s pioneers and reflects on his own longevity: “Se trata de trascender en la música” (It’s about transcending through music). — I.R.

Lana Del Rey shines as Delta Dawne in her role as a co-host of the rebellious Back Country Radio station in GTA. It’s only right she also delivered on the soundtrack, as LDR revels in a tragic romance for her “Crazy for You” ballad. Enter a Jason and Lucia romance scene from the campaign, with Lana providing the accompaniment. — M.S.

“50 Bands” is a braggadocious celebration of money, luxury, sexual confidence and unapologetic competition. The track is packed with personality as Latto and Flo Milli trade witty punchlines back and forth. Both ladies are flexing their looks, money and influence while taking shots at anyone they feel can’t keep up. When Latto and Flo Milli get together, “throw somе racks on it, make it plural.” — C.C.

Fuerza Regida trades corridos for a breezy reggaetón groove on “Suzuki,” a flirtatious, raunchy cut that finds the San Bernardino hitmakers venturing into new territory. Produced by Synthetic, the track glides on glossy electronic textures and a laid-back dembow bounce, while frontman Jesús Ortiz Paz delivers a string of shameless come-ons. From pole dancing and risqué fantasies to a cheeky reference to tusi (a.k.a. pink cocaine), the lyrics leave little to the imagination. The beat may be easygoing, but JOP clearly has no intention of behaving himself. — I.R.

“Aprovecha que tienes mi atención!” Anitta brings “Touch & Go” to life with this English- and Spanish-language version of “Vai Dar Caô,” originally featuring Ebony and Papatinho. Unfortunately, this version is missing those features — but Anitta still delivers the energy when it comes to casual attraction, sexual freedom and knowing how to leave someone wanting more.

On “Touch & Go,” Anitta enjoys the physical chemistry of a relationship, but has no interest in turning it into a deeper emotional commitment. And that sounds like a lot of y’all reading this! You get close, enjoy the moment and move on before the other person starts expecting anything more. A hot, flirtatious atmosphere can be fun for a while, but there’s no shame in wanting something more serious either. — C.C.

If half of Camila Cabello’s heart is in Havana, the other half lies in Miami. The dulcet “Sweet Like Candy” is a solid effort from CC — and like a good piece of candy, it’s not too heavy or sour, as the Fifth Harmony solo star sticks the landing with a fun, surface-level pop song. It also makes me think about where she has been in the last two years, with Cabello largely out of the pop scene since 2024’s C,XOXO. Time for a comeback, Camila. — M.S.

“Everybody getting’ loose!” Produced by Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo, Travis definitely found his pocket on this one. I can see this track growing in popularity over time, and it’s already one of my favorites on the album. You have to crank the volume all the way up for this one. There’s so much electronic-infused chaos packed into the production, making it feel like hip-hop built for the club. It fits flawlessly into the GTA universe. — C.C.

Gunna turned back the clock to the days long before he was running 5Ks and flexed a six-pack as a gym rat. The Atlanta native reunites with frequent collaborator Turbo on the production side for a hard-hitting trap banger that boasts a flow that will sound familiar to early Gunna fans from the days of his Drip or Drown and Drip Season series, when he was still rising through the rap ranks. — M.S.

For all the tenderness with which Kali Uchis and Helado Negro sing to each other, their message couldn’t be more blunt: lárgate (or “f–k off”). The Colombian American singer and Ecuadorian American musician explore the emotional contradictions of a relationship that’s run its course, alternating between wistful reflections and outright dismissal. The sweetness of their vocal interplay almost belies the bitterness of their words. — I.R.

Cardi B will always pop her s—t, and “Don’t Chart” is no different. From the Bronx all the way to Vice City, Cardi is talking her talk! The track marks her second release of 2026, following the arrival of “AH HA” in July. This is Cardi through and through: she’s “still poppin’, still winnin’, [and] you still hatin’.” The bouncy production is packed with flex after flex, touching on confidence, wealth, chart success and designer labels. Thank you, Cardi, for another boastful tongue-in-cheek anthem. — C.C.

“INTERNET $TAR” is a celebration of internet fame, individuality and the freedom to embrace who you are, even when the world doesn’t fully understand or appreciate you. Slayyyter presents herself as influential, memorable and impossible to replicate — which, if you know her, is exactly the point. — C.C.

I imagine Playboi Carti has thousands of songs in a folder on hard drives that he could lend out when needed. Whether it was Carti himself or right-hand producer F1LTHY, they made the right choice going with “Ahh Yea.” For Carti’s standards, “Ahh Yea” leans more into the poppier side of his artistry, and could easily be seen playing on the GTA radio while gamers cruise around Leonida. “Ahh Yea” seems like a holdover from the MUSIC era, and I wish we got more loosies like this from King Vamp. — M.S.

Argentine duo CA7RIEL & Paco Amoroso bring their irreverence to the dance floor on “Sexy Magic,” a bouncy, seductive electronic collaboration with British pop artist PinkPantheress, producer Fred again.. and French house veteran Étienne de Crécy. Riding a groovy bassline and shimmering synths, the track pairs Paco’s playful Spanish delivery with PinkPantheress’ breathy English vocals. Psychedelic around the edges and funky at its core, “Sexy Magic” sounds tailor-made for a neon-lit night cruising through Vice City. — I.R.

Travis Scott has been part of the Grand Theft Auto VI rollout every step of the way. Between attending events and making Cactus Jack x GTA merchandise collections, nobody’s been more hyped in hip-hop for the return of the iconic video game series than La Flame.

Scott makes a second appearance on the soundtrack with “Burn This S–t Down,” which sounds as if it has been the most creatively inspired he’s been in the last couple of years. It’s giving me that feeling of a hungry Cactus Jack in the mid-2010s, when he was pushing the boundaries of the genre and making his melodic rage part of hip-hop’s mainstream. That’s a good sign of things to come for La Flame, who should be in album mode for 2027.

“Burn” is a three-part rollercoaster, which he’s experimented with in the past (“SICKO MODE”). Scott plays with melody and then pushes the pace to bar up before turning the title into an eerie chant with an expansive sound that could score a film scene. The final portion will sound familiar to GTA VI gamers, as it was debuted during the explosive final mission of chapter one. — M.S.

New York is in the building! That opening line in the first verse, “You look prettier in person,” hits in this social media era. We all know what it’s like to meet someone in person after finding them online and being happy that they actually look like their pictures — or, in this case, look even better. Boogie, you did your thing with this one, my boy. This is about to go platinum in the crib: “I don’t wanna fight, I wanna dance tonight” — a perfect track for a late-night drive through Vice City.— C.C.

Dua Lipa has proven to be the queen of a soundtrack when she dished out the top 10 Hot 100 bop “Dance the Night” for Barbie in 2023. With an intro that seems to draw from Phil Collins’ “Don’t Lose My Number” and later interpolates KISS’ “I Was Made for Lovin’ You,” the pop star has a penchant for taking songs of yesteryear and making them digestible for today’s audiences. “Go Easy” is no different for the hitmaker, as Dua clears the decks and gears up to launch a new era in the first quarter of ’27. — M.S.

“Flower in a Hurricane” is the preeminent song from GTA VI. In a short time, it’s already essentially become the video game’s theme song, providing the soundtrack to key scenes, clips and compilations going viral on social media. Justice meshes its EDM roots with King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard’s rock while SZA and Kevin Parker join forces to sing about surviving the storm to make it out alive on the other side. It perfectly balances the angst of everything falling apart at any moment on the journey to Vice City glory. — M.S.

#3275. 10 'Find Hub' Hacks Every Android User Should Know

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

Google's Find Hub app isn't just for tracking your lost smartphone. Over the past year, Google has consistently added features to manage your belongings, share your location with loved ones, and locate lost devices. Find Hub can now notify you when you've left your device or your tracker behind. Plus, you can use Gemini to remember where you left items, even without a tracker attached. Behind the scenes, there are even more hidden settings and features to help track your devices and make it easier to retrieve them in case they are stolen or misplaced. If you use Find Hub, you need to know about these 10 hacks.

This month, Google finally added Left Behind notifications to Android trackers—but you have to enable the feature manually. AirTags users should be familiar with this feature already. When you leave your tracker or device behind, and exit the location range, you’ll receive a notification that you left without your item. You need to enable this feature on a per-device basis. Go to Find Hub and select a device. Tap the settings gear icon next to the device's name, and enable Notify when left behind. While you’re here, go to Add location to add familiar locations where you don’t want to get a notification (like your home or workspace). Otherwise, Find Hub may spam you with left behind alerts.

There’s a hidden feature in the Find Hub app that helps you keep track of things without actually using a Bluetooth tracker. You can simply ask Gemini to remember where you put things, and it will show up in the Find Hub app. To use it, pull up Gemini and say something like, “Remember in Find Hub that the passport is in the downstairs wardrobe,” or “I’ve kept the spare car keys behind the garage door.”

You can then ask Gemini, “Where did I keep my passport?” and it will tell you. If you change the location of an item, just ask Gemini to update it for you. When you go to the Remembered tab, you’ll see the location of all remembered items. You can also add items manually here using the Add button.

Some Android smartphones can remain findable for several hours after they've been switched off or their batteries have run out. If you’re using a supported device (like the latest Pixel series smartphone), you can use a hardware feature to track the location using Google’s mesh network, relying on nearby devices (similar to how Android tags work).

To make sure this feature is enabled, go to Find Hub, and tap Find your offline devices. Here, make sure that either With network in busy places only or With network everywhere is selected.

If you’re using a tracker in your car, luggage, or on your keys, you might want to share location access with your spouse or family members. Find Hub has a feature called "Share Ownership" that lets you share the tracker details with up to 10 people. Only the location of your tracker is shared, not your personal device.

To set it up, go to Find Hub, and choose the tracker or accessory that you want to share. Tap the Share Ownership button and follow the on-screen instructions to share the invite link via a messaging app or using Quick Share. Once the recipient taps Accept, you’ll get a notification. Go to the device settings in Find Hub and tap the Confirm button to enable location sharing.

You can quickly share your live location with your friends or loved ones using Google Messages. Open a conversation, tap the Attachment icon, and choose Real-time location. Set the duration and tap Send.

If you don’t like using the Messages app, you can do so directly from Find Hub. Go to the People tab at the bottom of the screen, and tap the Plus icon. Choose the duration and select a contact to share the location with, then tap the Get Link button to copy the link. You can then share it via any messaging app of your choice.

You might have a Find Hub tracker in your luggage to help keep tabs on your bags. But you don't have to be the only one privy to its location. If your airline loses that luggage, you can temporarily share its location with your airline to help you retrieve it. This is an official feature, too: Google partnered with multiple airlines to make this data sharing easier. From the Find Hub, choose your tracker. Tap the Share Item Location button, and then tap Share Item Location again. Copy the generated web link and share it with your airline using the app or support page. The link will automatically expire in seven days, so you don't have to worry about your airline continuing to monitor your luggage's location long after your flight.

Find Hub uses a mesh network of supported Android devices to securely locate your lost device or tag. But by default, it waits until multiple Android devices detect the location of the lost device. This works well if you've lost the device in crowded areas, but it can increase your wait time if you lose it somewhere remote. Luckily, there is a hidden setting that triggers location sharing even if a single device reports its location. Go to Settings > Google > All services > Find Hub > Find your offline devices and select With network everywhere instead of With network in busy places only.

If you’ve lost your smartphone, you don’t need to rush to a computer or a website to track it. Borrow someone’s Android smartphone and head into their Find Hub. Tap Sign in as guest and sign in with your Google account associated with your device, then find and select your device in the account. If requested, enter the PIN that you’ve previously set up. You can now track the device’s location, get directions to the device, or play a sound to help track the device if it’s nearby. If the device is truly lost, you can use the Mark as Lost feature to remotely lock your device.

Map-based tracking is helpful in getting to the general vicinity of your lost device. But your smartphone or tracker is hidden; finding it may require precision tracking. Many newer trackers like the Pixel Tag come with an ultra-wideband chip that helps you find the exact location of the tracker, given you are nearby. This also works on Pixel smartphones (Pixel 8 Pro series and above) and Samsung Galaxy devices (S21 and above, Plus and Ultra models only).

When using this feature, make sure you have Bluetooth enabled on your smartphone, then open Find Hub. Choose your tracker, and tap Find Nearby. Follow the on-screen instructions to locate the nearby device. You can also tap Play Sound to make the location process easier.

If you think your Android smartphone is lost or stolen, don’t rush to erase all data. While a remote factory reset is great for protecting your data, it also removes the device from your account. It’s best to try to get the device back. Two-factor authentication (or a passkey) on your Google account, along with a biometric lock on your smartphone, will protect the data itself.

Go to the Find Hub website, or use Find Hub on someone else’s phone in guest mode. Choose your device, and instead of Factory Reset, choose Mark as Lost. Here, you’ll see an option to enter a message. Type an alternative contact number, and a message to help recover the device.

#3274. Tidal Is the First Streaming Service to Ban AI Music

Tidal has announced an ambitious plan to ban all music wholly generated by artificial intelligence.

On Dec. 9, the streaming service will start rejecting uploads of all music made with AI, and removing any that are currently on the platform. Tidal head Robert Anderson stated that all AI tracks will be gone by the beginning of 2027.

The new policy will apply only to music made completely with AI tools like Suno, Lyria, and Udio. Tidal will continue to allow tracks made with the assistance of AI tools, “but not the sole outputs” of them.

As Anderson noted on X, this decision makes Tidal the first digital streaming platform to ban AI music, and he pointedly encouraged others in the industry to “follow suit.” The move comes after Tidal began labeling and demonetizing AI-generated tracks over the summer.

The proliferation of AI music on streaming platforms has caused numerous headaches for artists and labels over the past few years. While much of it goes unnoticed — Tidal estimated 96 percent of the AI songs it’s already flagged have garnered zero streams over the last 90 days — tracks that do catch on can divert streams and royalties from working artists.

There are also fraud concerns, whether it’s bots streaming AI-generated music, or scammers uploading AI tracks under the names of actual artists. Tidal said it’s already taken down over 65,000 such tracks “flagged for suspected artist-name impersonation.

“Wholly AI-generated music intended to mislead listeners and impersonate artists is another serious problem that has only increased in scale: It diverts streams and royalties away from the artists, and confuses fans,” Tidal said in its statement.

Speaking to the scale of the AI music problem, Tidal estimated that there are 27 to 29 million AI tracks on its platform now (about six percent of its total catalog). Additionally, the company said 43 percent of all uploads from the past 90 days were flagged as wholly AI-generated. Anderson said the platform expects to reject anywhere between 80,000 to 85,000 songs per day once the new policy goes into effect.  Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

While Tidal’s reject-and-remove policy is a novel step in the effort to combat AI slop, effective enforcement could pose some challenges. Earlier this year, DistroKid, the largest music distribution platform by volume, accidentally removed a bunch of real music, made by real artists, while doing mass takedowns in response to a copyright infringement lawsuit filed by Universal Music Group. (DistroKid apologized for the accidental takedowns, and has denied UMG’s accusations.)

Tidal has, however, at least been able to test out its detection tools thanks to its efforts to flag and demonetize AI music over the past few months. A rep for Tidal did not return a request for comment about the success rate of its detection tools, but streamer’s tech partner, Ircam Amplify, boasts 99 percent accuracy and false positives under one percent.  Trending Stories Billy Ray Cyrus Shares Snapshots From Miley’s Wedding: ‘Beautiful’ to See Family ‘United by Love’ U2 Will Bring Their ‘Greatest Show on Earth’ Stadium Tour to North America in 2027 Chris Christie to Republicans: ‘I Don’t Want to Hear Your Whining’ Anthem Singer Apologizes for ‘O Canada’ Flub at Leafs-Islanders Game

Along with using these tools to determine whether a song is made with AI, Tidal said would ban distributors from “delivering these tracks to us” and would “reject delivers if their metadata says they were generated solely using AI tools.”

Tidal said its AI policy “was designed to provide a great experience for listeners, while protecting the authenticity and livelihoods of artists and rightsholders. Tidal will always fight for artists to get paid more. Everything in this update comes back to that. If you make music, you should be able to put it on Tidal knowing it won’t be buried under tracks no one asked for, or copied by someone pretending to be you. We’ll keep sharing what we find and we’ll keep acting on it.”

#3272. The Wallet-Sized Xteink X4 Pro Is Lifehacker's E-Reader Gift of the Year, and It's on Sale for Black Friday

I've read more than 30 books in the past year, all of them on an e-reader with a screen roughly the size of a credit card. If you think that sounds untenable, I say: Don't knock it 'til you've tried it. Once you're immersed in a book, you'll find the size doesn't matter, and the convenience of being able to slip it into any pocket and forget it's there means you need never be without it.

Right now, the Xteink X4 Pro, the best tiny e-reader I've tried so far—and Lifehacker's pick for the 2026 E-Reader Gift of the Year—is on its best sale yet for Black Friday: When ordered directly from Xteink, you'll save 15% off the usual $99 price, bringing it down to $84. This is the cheapest e-reader with a light and a touchscreen that you can buy right now, and it's well worth the money.

The X4 Pro is the newest and best e-reader from Xteink, the Chinese tech startup that turned the e-reading world upside down last year with the launch of the original X4 pocket e-reader. While the X4 Pro is the same size as the basic X4 Classic, it adds two big upgrades—a temperature-adjustable front light and a touchscreen—plus a faster processor and more memory. As a result, it costs a bit more, but you can pick one at a $15 discount right now. (Even at full retail, the X4 Pro is $50 cheaper than the entry-level Kindle after its recent price increase—and even considering the Kindle's current Black Friday discount).

Meanwhile, if you're a reader who prioritizes the crispest text over conveniences like a front light, the 4.3-inch Xteink X4 Classic and the smaller 3.7-inch Xteink X3 are about $30 less during Amazon's own Black Friday sale.

As much as I love them, these minuscule e-readers aren't for everyone. Some may indeed find the screen too small (though if you've ever read a book on a phone, the experience is similar). Then there's the fact that they can't load your existing libraries of Kindle books; you'll need to source copies of e-books lacking Digital Rights Management (DRM) software. But if you can jump those hurdles, you might just discover it's the weirdest, most lovable piece of tech you've used in years.

#3271. Signal now blocks screenshots on iPhone to stop Siri AI from seeing chats

Popular secure messaging app Signal has rolled out a new update that automatically disables screenshots for the sake of blocking Siri AI from reading your chats. Here are the details.

Signal’s latest app update on iPhone disables a key system feature: taking screenshots.

As Signal told Reuters, that’s because Apple doesn’t currently provide better tools for iOS developers to safeguard app content from Siri AI and third-party AI agents.

By default, users who update and try to take a screenshot will see a message that says: “Screenshot prevented by ‘Block Siri AI’ setting.”

Signal now blocks in-app screenshots on iPhone to keep Siri AI from reading chatsIt’s a new toggle in settings that’s on by default, but can be turned offNo equivalent for its Mac app pic.twitter.com/ImsinqMNPq

Here’s exactly what that toggle does, per the in-app settings:

Prevent Siri AI from scanning Signal content. This will also block you from taking screenshots in the app and App Switcher.

Apple already lets you block Siri AI from accessing whichever apps you manually exclude, and that became even easier in iOS 27.2. But rather than directing users to that system option, Signal seems to believe it needed to take action itself with this update.

What do you think of Signal’s latest move? Let us know in the comments.

#3270. Cher’s Victory in Royalties War Under Fire as Mary Bono Pushes for Reversal

Sonny Bono’s widow, Mary Bono, is appealing her defeat in a four-year royalties war with Cher, arguing in a brief filed Monday that a federal judge erred last year in ruling that Cher’s 1978 divorce agreement with Sonny Bono took precedence over federal copyright law. Mary Bono contends that the federal Copyright Act entitles her and Sonny’s children to reclaim the 50 percent share of his songwriting royalties awarded to Cher in the divorce.

In his ruling last year, U.S. District Court Judge John Kronstadt found that Cher’s marital settlement agreement entitled her to a 50 percent share of Sonny’s composition royalties, rather than an interest in the copyrights themselves. As such, he found that her claim was protected by state contract law and not subject to the termination rules of the Copyright Act.

In the divorce settlement, Sonny awarded Cher the 50 percent cut of his composition royalties for hit songs including “I Got You Babe” and “The Beat Goes On.” Cher also got a 50 percent share of the musical recordings they made together. In court filings, Cher’s lawyers said Mary had “secretly” begun diverting Cher’s royalties to herself and Sonny’s other heirs after using the termination provisions of the Copyright Act. Cher sued, and the court determined her grant was untouchable.

In the new 33-page appellate brief obtained by Rolling Stone, Mary and her lawyers sharply criticize the ruling. They argue the lower court “struggled with the concept that copyright terminations preempted Sonny’s right to contract freely and bargain away his heirs’ rights.” They say copyright termination “trumps the common law’s freedom to contract.”

“Sonny could not have alienated Mary’s right, as his widow, to the post-termination copyright interests when he entered into the MSA in 1978. Despite any language to the contrary in the MSA, all of the reverted rights, including the right to receive royalties, belong to the heirs,” the brief, filed in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, states. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

“The District Court focused extensively on family law questions and, in particular, spousal support, even though the parties agree that the MSA is a contract like any other,” the filing reads. “This unfortunately led the District Court to err by failing to acknowledge that the federal Copyright Act preempts state law on the issue of copyright terminations.”

Attempts to reach Cher’s lead lawyer on the lawsuit were not immediately successful Tuesday. The lawyer, Peter J. Anderson, previously argued in court that the Copyright Act was clear, and that by the time Sonny and Cher signed their divorce settlement in August of 1978, they were “sophisticated people” represented by “sophisticated lawyers.”

He said Sonny and Cher knew during negotiations that “I Got You Babe” and “Bang Bang” were big hits. “They knew this. They also knew that the 1976 Copyright Act was in effect and that on January 1, 1978, it had a termination right. So, when they said Cher gets 50 percent of all royalties from all sources, that includes under the replacement publishing agreements when they terminate the initial publishing agreements,” Anderson argued to the court. “These songs were already tested by the marketplace. These sophisticated people already knew about termination rights.” Trending Stories Billy Ray Cyrus Shares Snapshots From Miley’s Wedding: ‘Beautiful’ to See Family ‘United by Love’ U2 Will Bring Their ‘Greatest Show on Earth’ Stadium Tour to North America in 2027 Chris Christie to Republicans: ‘I Don’t Want to Hear Your Whining’ Anthem Singer Apologizes for ‘O Canada’ Flub at Leafs-Islanders Game

Cher’s side will have a chance to respond before the appeals court issues any ruling.

Cher, 80, rose to fame alongside Sonny in the 1960s before building a decades-long solo career that brought her Grammy, Oscar, and Emmy wins. Sonny died in a skiing accident in 1998, leaving Mary in charge of his estate. His music publishing grants became eligible for termination beginning in 2018.

#3269. These Are the Best Early Black Friday Deals on Kindles and E-Readers

Amazon's Black Friday sale kicked off today, which means it's a good time to score some of the year's best prices on e-readers. Timing your purchase is now a bigger deal than ever (so to speak), as Amazon recently raised the price of basically every Kindle by $50 or more due to the ongoing RAM crisis.

Because of this, the prices aren't nearly as low as they were last year, but now is still the time to get a decent discount on a Kindle Paperwhite or Colorsoft—but if you'd rather read differently, you can also save big on a few worthy Kindle alternatives. Here are your e-reader best bets in the lead-up to Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

The Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is the best e-reader for most people. An upgraded version of the basic Kindle, the Paperwhite adds a larger screen, temperature-adjustable lighting, water resistance, and better battery life—and if you opt for the Signature Edition, you also get double the storage and no lock screen ads. Earlier this year, it jumped in price to $250, even before the company introduced a new model—but you can get the 2024 model for $179.99, 28% off the new list price.

If you want a great Kindle but you don't care about paying extra for more storage or getting rid of lock screen ads, the non-Signature Edition of the Kindle Paperwhite is also a great buy right now. The 2024 model has been discounted to $129.99 from the list price of $199.99. It's available in standard black, Jade, or Raspberry colors.

If you don't need the bells and whistles of the Paperwhite, you can also pick up the standard Kindle. It's still a very capable device, with good lighting, 16GB of onboard storage, and the ability to hook up your Bluetooth speakers to listen to Audible audiobooks. The standard Kindle, which now retails for $150, is marked down to $119.99, making it the cheapest Kindle option. Though I think it makes more sense to spend $10 more on the Signature Edition, this is the way to go if you want the cute Matcha color.

If you like to read comics or you just appreciate looking at your book covers in full color, the 2024 Kindle Colorsoft is also at a strong 41% discount for Black Friday, bringing it down to around $170. For $10 less than the Paperwhite Signature edition, you get all the same perks (including an ad-free experience) and a color e-ink screen that's great for reading magazines, graphic novels, and manga. Color e-ink isn't for everyone, but if it's for you, the Colorsoft has the best color screen on the market. For an extra $10, the Colorsoft Kids Edition adds a case, a yearlong subscription to Kindle Kids+, and an extended warranty.

If you're looking for a combination e-reader and e-notebook, the Kindle Scribe is a great option. With a larger screen than Amazon's other e-readers, it offers all the benefits of the Paperwhite but adds support for the excellent Premium Pen stylus, allowing you to take notes in your Amazon e-books or create handwritten documents that you can later convert to text using the onboard AI tools. The 32GB black-and-white version of the Kindle Scribe is currently $349.99, while the Colorsoft version will run you $449.99. Both of these are the newest models, released in 2025.

The new Kindle Scribe Colorsoft has all the same great features of the black-and-white version discussed above, but adds a full-color e-ink display. Combined with the large 11-inch screen, this makes it a great device for reading comics or magazine articles as they were meant to be read, or marking up PDFs using the included Premium Pen. This device usually costs a hefty $630, but the current Black Friday sale cuts $180 off of that price.

If you want to step outside of the Amazon ecosystem, the Kobo Libra Colour is a good bet. Discounted $30 to $229.99 at Best Buy, it's currently pricier than the Kindle Colorsoft, but you get a bit more for your money. While most of the specs are similar (they both use the same Kaleido 3 screen and offer 32GB of storage), the Kobo supports a stylus, so you can jot down notes in your books or keep a digital journal. It also has physical page-turn buttons, which the Colorsoft lacks.

If you don't want to be tied to the Amazon ecosystem and/or you're looking for a device that's a bit more portable, consider the Viwoods AiPaper Reader, currently marked down to $200, its lowest price ever. It's got a 6.13-inch screen, so it's the same size and shape as your phone, and it has a crisp e-ink screen with a strong (if not temperature-adjustable) front light and 128GB of onboard storage. The best part is, it runs on an open Android system, so you can install multiple reading apps, including Kindle, Nook, Kobo, and Libby, and keep all of your books in one place. (Check out my review of the Viwoods AiPaper Reader for more—it's a nifty little device.)

If you don't have a large Kindle library, you're moderately tech-savvy, and you praise portability above all else, I can't recommend Xteink's line of e-readers more highly. The 4.3-inch Xteink X4 Classic is at its lowest price ever, coming in at just under $55, around $34 off the list price. Meanwhile, the smaller 3.7-inch Xteink X3 is about a dollar more; that's a less-generous 19% discount. I own both, and while the Classic is definitely worth the current sale price, I actually prefer the form factor of the smaller X3 (currently $55.72), which is about the size of a library card.

For about $30 more than the X4 Classic, you can upgrade to the Xteink X4 Pro, which happens to be Lifehacker's e-reader Gift of the Year pick. It offers all the perks of the other Xteink devices, with two critical quality-of-life upgrades: A touchscreen for easier navigation, and a temperature-adjustable front light so you can read it in a dark room. (Less obviously, it also has a slightly faster processor that makes the whole thing feel a little snappier.) Right now, the X4 Pro is at its lowest price ever when ordered directly from Xteink: $84, or around 15% off the usual $99 price.

If you're feeling tentative about trusting a seemingly no-name Chinese tech brand, read more about the devices in my review, or listen to the collected wisdom of the tens of thousands of people in the bustling r/xteink Reddit group.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

#3266. Atomically Thin Materials Significantly Shrink Qubits

MIT researchers use 2D materials for capacitors in quantum circuits in an effort to scale processors

Superconducting quantum processor and its microwave packaging.

Quantum computing is a devilishly complex technology, with many technical hurdles impacting its development. Of these challenges two critical issues stand out: miniaturization and qubit quality.

IBM has adopted the superconducting qubit road map of reaching a 1,121-qubit processor by 2023, leading to the expectation that 1,000 qubits with today’s qubit form factor is feasible. However, current approaches will require very large chips (50 millimeters on a side, or larger) at the scale of small wafers, or the use of chiplets on multichip modules. While this approach will work, the aim is to attain a better path toward scalability.

Now researchers at MIT have been able to both reduce the size of the qubits and done so in a way that reduces the interference that occurs between neighboring qubits. The MIT researchers have increased the number of superconducting qubits that can be added onto a device by a factor of 100.

“We are addressing both qubit miniaturization and quality,” said William Oliver, the director for the Center for Quantum Engineering at MIT. “Unlike conventional transistor scaling, where only the number really matters, for qubits, large numbers are not sufficient, they must also be high-performance. Sacrificing performance for qubit number is not a useful trade in quantum computing. They must go hand in hand.”

The key to this big increase in qubit density and reduction of interference comes down to the use of two-dimensional materials, in particular the 2D insulator hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). The MIT researchers demonstrated that a few atomic monolayers of hBN can be stacked to form the insulator in the capacitors of a superconducting qubit.

Just like other capacitors, the capacitors in these superconducting circuits take the form of a sandwich in which an insulator material is sandwiched between two metal plates. The big difference for these capacitors is that the superconducting circuits can operate only at extremely low temperatures—less than 0.02 degrees above absolute zero (-273.15 °C).

Superconducting qubits are measured at temperatures as low as 20 millikelvin in a dilution refrigerator.Nathan Fiske/MIT

In that environment, insulating materials that are available for the job, such as PE-CVD silicon oxide or silicon nitride, have quite a few defects that are too lossy for quantum computing applications. To get around these material shortcomings, most superconducting circuits use what are called coplanar capacitors. In these capacitors, the plates are positioned laterally to one another, rather than on top of one another.

As a result, the intrinsic silicon substrate below the plates and to a smaller degree the vacuum above the plates serve as the capacitor dielectric. Intrinsic silicon is chemically pure and therefore has few defects, and the large size dilutes the electric field at the plate interfaces, all of which leads to a low-loss capacitor. The lateral size of each plate in this open-face design ends up being quite large (typically 100 by 100 micrometers) in order to achieve the required capacitance.

In an effort to move away from the large lateral configuration, the MIT researchers embarked on a search for an insulator that has very few defects and is compatible with superconducting capacitor plates.

“We chose to study hBN because it is the most widely used insulator in 2D material research due to its cleanliness and chemical inertness,” said colead author Joel Wang, a research scientist in the Engineering Quantum Systems group of the MIT Research Laboratory for Electronics.

On either side of the hBN, the MIT researchers used the 2D superconducting material, niobium diselenide. One of the trickiest aspects of fabricating the capacitors was working with the niobium diselenide, which oxidizes in seconds when exposed to air, according to Wang. This necessitates that the assembly of the capacitor occur in a glove box filled with argon gas.

While this would seemingly complicate the scaling up of the production of these capacitors, Wang doesn’t regard this as a limiting factor.

“What determines the quality factor of the capacitor are the two interfaces between the two materials,” said Wang. “Once the sandwich is made, the two interfaces are “sealed” and we don’t see any noticeable degradation over time when exposed to the atmosphere.”

This lack of degradation is because around 90 percent of the electric field is contained within the sandwich structure, so the oxidation of the outer surface of the niobium diselenide does not play a significant role anymore. This ultimately makes the capacitor footprint much smaller, and it accounts for the reduction in cross talk between the neighboring qubits.

“The main challenge for scaling up the fabrication will be the wafer-scale growth of hBN and 2D superconductors like [niobium diselenide], and how one can do wafer-scale stacking of these films,” added Wang.

Wang believes that this research has shown 2D hBN to be a good insulator candidate for superconducting qubits. He says that the groundwork the MIT team has done will serve as a road map for using other hybrid 2D materials to build superconducting circuits.

Dexter Johnson is a contributing editor at IEEE Spectrum, with a focus on nanotechnology.

#3265. If You Loved 'The Diplomat,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

The Diplomat is a show that loves mess (complimentary). Kate Wyler (Keri Russel) is a mess in many ways, and almost every major character is at emotional, moral, or intellectual loose ends. This would all be in good fun if these characters weren’t also some of the most powerful people in the world—presidents, prime ministers, and the high-level politicians and diplomats that serve them.

If you’ve been following the Wylers’ emotional journey up the power ladder as Kate navigates her role as the U.S. ambassador to the United Kingdom during what could be described as tumultuous times (and you’ve watched all our series streamalikes), allow me to suggest the one perfect movie that delivers similar vibes: 2009's In the Loop.

Released in 2009, In the Loop doesn’t have the modern edge of The Diplomat, but it perfectly captures a similar sense that international diplomacy is being conducted by people with an affinity for chaos. It’s actually a spinoff from a British TV series from the same co-writer/director, Armando Iannucci: The Thick of It. Many of the characters and situations are based on some of the people actually running the U.K., but you don’t need to be familiar with the show or the real history to enjoy the heck out of this movie. That goes double for Peter Capaldi’s absolutely ferocious performance as Malcolm Tucker, a man so creative with his profanity that many of his F-bombs will live rent-free in your head for years to come.

When a not-so-bright minister in the U.K. government (played by Tom Hollander) makes some dimwitted remarks that threaten to blow up Britain's carefully crafted diplomatic messaging around potential military adventures in the Middle East, Tucker (the prime minister's director of communications) has to tamp down the growing chaos that results. This eventually requires a contingent of British diplomats and officials to head to Washington, where they are quickly overwhelmed by the superpower vibes they encounter.

It’s a more profane, faster-paced, and outright comedic story than The Diplomat, but it’s also easy to imagine most of the characters showing up on that show. The film also shares that same sense of controlled chaos that drives The Diplomat—the idea that a handful of tired, dedicated people are continuously racing around to prevent World War III even as dumber and more powerful people keep creating new crises. If Kate Wyler’s constant state of exhausted anxiety is your jam, you’ll love this movie. Stream In the Loop on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

Want more cynical diplomats, secret plans, and international skulduggery with a side of personal emotional crises? Here are a few more movies fans of The Diplomat will love.

If you want a sense of what actual back-channel diplomacy is like, watch Ben Affleck’s Best Picture winner Argo, from 2012. Based on the remarkable true story of how six U.S. diplomats were rescued from Tehran during the Iran Hostage Crisis under cover of a fake sci-fi movie production, the film has the snappy energy and fast pace of The Diplomat combined with real-world danger. You can easily imagine Kate and Hal (Rufus Sewell) being part of the secret, off-the-books conversations that brought what’s known as the Canadian Caper into reality. Stream Argo on Paramount Plus or rent it on Prime Video.

If your favorite parts of The Diplomat are the schemes various players (mostly Kate and Hal) get up to in their efforts to shape world diplomacy and history to their liking, Wag the Dog is a good bet. When a sex scandal threatens to swing the Presidential election away from the incumbent, a spin doctor (Robert De Niro) wades in to save the day by convincing a top Hollywood producer (Dustin Hoffman) to “produce” a fake war in Albania to distract the American public. It’s equal parts funny, compelling, and depressingly instructive, and fans of the show will love the back-channel hijinks. Rent Wag the Dog on Prime Video.

One of the great things about The Diplomat is watching Kate Wyler, a smart and capable woman who generally knows more than anyone else in the room. If that’s the dynamic that grabs you, The Contender is the overlooked gem for you. When the vice president dies unexpectedly, the President (Jeff Bridges) nominates Senator Laine Hanson (Joan Allen) to take the post. A conservative senator (Gary Oldman) opposes her nomination and launches a smear campaign to derail her confirmation. There are dirty tricks and secret deals, and in the middle of it all, Allen’s terrific performance as a woman who refuses to back down in the face of sexist, unfair attacks. Stream The Contender on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Apple TV.

Nicole Kidman plays an interpreter at the United Nations, a woman who has a unique heritage and linguistic knowledge. When she overhears an assassination plot in an obscure dialect, she becomes embroiled in a dangerous game of espionage and high-stakes diplomacy as she races to prevent disaster (and keep herself alive). The Interpreter is a more serious and much more tense story, but it delves into the background work that makes the global system function, which puts it right in the sweet spot for fans of The Diplomat. Stream The Interpreter on Netflix, or rent it on Prime Video.

This might not seem like a match at first glance—a comedic treatment of the power struggle that followed the death of Soviet Premier Josef Stalin in 1953—but it absolutely is. Making a farce out of the political wrangling among the members of the Central Committee, the film has the same spirit as The Diplomat, showing that the people in charge are a bunch of schemers, tricksters, dummies, and sociopaths. Watching them run around making deals and angling for advantage offers the same energy as the show. Plus, it’s just plain hilarious. Stream The Death of Stalin on Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3264. iOS 27 has clever new Messages feature I’ve been using a lot

iOS 27 gives the Messages app a variety of welcome upgrades, including one I’ve found myself using a lot: a Smart Reply feature that’s now personalized to the user’s writing style.

When the first wave of Apple Intelligence features were announced in 2024, one that I immediately thought sounded useful was Smart Reply.

The idea behind Smart Reply is simple. Rather than needing to manually type out replies in Messages and Mail, your iPhone can offer prewritten replies you can choose and send with a couple taps.

Great in theory, but the ‘Smart’ part of Smart Reply struggled to materialize in iOS 18.

Fortunately, with a key Apple Intelligence upgrade in iOS 27, the new version of the feature finally lives up to its name. Per Apple:

Smart Reply in Mail and Messages can now draw on a user’s personalized writing style.

Before, Smart Reply would look at the context of a conversation to craft its suggestions. But now, it also aims to match your writing style, punctuation, and tone.

In iOS 18, I almost never used Smart Reply. That’s because despite being fine at suggesting replies that technically worked, those suggestions didn’t sound like me at all.

That’s changed in iOS 27. Smart Reply now consistently impresses me. It no longer offers generic responses that sound like AI wrote them. Instead, its suggestions actually fit with my normal style of communication.

The only drawback is that right now, you’ll only ever see two Smart Reply suggestions. If Apple expanded the feature by letting you scroll horizontally through more options, I suspect I’d use Smart Reply even more.

Have you been using iOS 27’s Smart Reply feature in Messages? Let us know in the comments.

#3263. How AI Will Change Chip Design

Artificial intelligence’s promise and potential for the semiconductor industry

Rina Diane Caballar is a contributing editor covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment.

An array of semiconductor wafers are ready to be made into chips.

The end of Moore’s Law is looming. Engineers and designers can do only so much to miniaturize transistors and pack as many of them as possible into chips. So they’re turning to other approaches to chip design, incorporating technologies like AI into the process.

Samsung, for instance, is adding AI to its memory chips to enable processing in memory, thereby saving energy and speeding up machine learning. Speaking of speed, Google’s TPU V4 AI chip has doubled its processing power compared with that of its previous version.

But AI holds still more promise and potential for the semiconductor industry. To better understand how AI is set to revolutionize chip design, we spoke with Heather Gorr, senior product manager for MathWorks’ MATLAB platform.

How is AI currently being used to design the next generation of chips?

Heather Gorr: AI is such an important technology because it’s involved in most parts of the cycle, including the design and manufacturing process. There’s a lot of important applications here, even in the general process engineering where we want to optimize things. I think defect detection is a big one at all phases of the process, especially in manufacturing. But even thinking ahead in the design process, [AI now plays a significant role] when you’re designing the light and the sensors and all the different components. There’s a lot of anomaly detection and fault mitigation that you really want to consider.

Then, thinking about the logistical modeling that you see in any industry, there is always planned downtime that you want to mitigate; but you also end up having unplanned downtime. So, looking back at that historical data of when you’ve had those moments where maybe it took a bit longer than expected to manufacture something, you can take a look at all of that data and use AI to try to identify the proximate cause or to see something that might jump out even in the processing and design phases. We think of AI oftentimes as a predictive tool, or as a robot doing something, but a lot of times you get a lot of insight from the data through AI.

What are the benefits of using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Historically, we’ve seen a lot of physics-based modeling, which is a very intensive process. We want to do a reduced order model, where instead of solving such a computationally expensive and extensive model, we can do something a little cheaper. You could create a surrogate model, so to speak, of that physics-based model, use the data, and then do your parameter sweeps, your optimizations, your Monte Carlo simulations using the surrogate model. That takes a lot less time computationally than solving the physics-based equations directly. So, we’re seeing that benefit in many ways, including the efficiency and economy that are the results of iterating quickly on the experiments and the simulations that will really help in the design.

So it’s like having a digital twin in a sense?

Gorr: Exactly. That’s pretty much what people are doing, where you have the physical system model and the experimental data. Then, in conjunction, you have this other model that you could tweak and tune and try different parameters and experiments that let sweep through all of those different situations and come up with a better design in the end.

So, it’s going to be more efficient and, as you said, cheaper?

Gorr: Yeah, definitely. Especially in the experimentation and design phases, where you’re trying different things. That’s obviously going to yield dramatic cost savings if you’re actually manufacturing and producing [the chips]. You want to simulate, test, experiment as much as possible without making something using the actual process engineering.

We’ve talked about the benefits. How about the drawbacks?

Gorr: The [AI-based experimental models] tend to not be as accurate as physics-based models. Of course, that’s why you do many simulations and parameter sweeps. But that’s also the benefit of having that digital twin, where you can keep that in mind—it’s not going to be as accurate as that precise model that we’ve developed over the years.

Both chip design and manufacturing are system intensive; you have to consider every little part. And that can be really challenging. It’s a case where you might have models to predict something and different parts of it, but you still need to bring it all together.

One of the other things to think about too is that you need the data to build the models. You have to incorporate data from all sorts of different sensors and different sorts of teams, and so that heightens the challenge.

How can engineers use AI to better prepare and extract insights from hardware or sensor data?

Gorr: We always think about using AI to predict something or do some robot task, but you can use AI to come up with patterns and pick out things you might not have noticed before on your own. People will use AI when they have high-frequency data coming from many different sensors, and a lot of times it’s useful to explore the frequency domain and things like data synchronization or resampling. Those can be really challenging if you’re not sure where to start.

One of the things I would say is, use the tools that are available. There’s a vast community of people working on these things, and you can find lots of examples [of applications and techniques] on GitHub or MATLAB Central, where people have shared nice examples, even little apps they’ve created. I think many of us are buried in data and just not sure what to do with it, so definitely take advantage of what’s already out there in the community. You can explore and see what makes sense to you, and bring in that balance of domain knowledge and the insight you get from the tools and AI.

What should engineers and designers consider when using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Think through what problems you’re trying to solve or what insights you might hope to find, and try to be clear about that. Consider all of the different components, and document and test each of those different parts. Consider all of the people involved, and explain and hand off in a way that is sensible for the whole team.

How do you think AI will affect chip designers’ jobs?

Gorr: It’s going to free up a lot of human capital for more advanced tasks. We can use AI to reduce waste, to optimize the materials, to optimize the design, but then you still have that human involved whenever it comes to decision-making. I think it’s a great example of people and technology working hand in hand. It’s also an industry where all people involved—even on the manufacturing floor—need to have some level of understanding of what’s happening, so this is a great industry for advancing AI because of how we test things and how we think about them before we put them on the chip.

How do you envision the future of AI and chip design?

Gorr: It’s very much dependent on that human element—involving people in the process and having that interpretable model. We can do many things with the mathematical minutiae of modeling, but it comes down to how people are using it, how everybody in the process is understanding and applying it. Communication and involvement of people of all skill levels in the process are going to be really important. We’re going to see less of those superprecise predictions and more transparency of information, sharing, and that digital twin—not only using AI but also using our human knowledge and all of the work that many people have done over the years.

Rina Diane Caballar is a writer covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment. An IEEE Spectrum contributing editor, she's a former software engineer based in New Zealand.

#3261. HomeKit Weekly: Lafaer’s 5-in-1 presence sensor fixes an annoying automation in Apple Home

Motion-based automations are generally straightforward in Apple Home. The only carve-out is lighting, because some rooms are hard to judge by time of day alone. Depending on the windows and placement against the sun, some rooms might need light-based automations earlier in the day than others. The Lafaer 5-in-1 presence sensor fixes that with a light sensor most motion sensors lack, along with mmWave radar.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

A standard motion sensor uses PIR, which only detects movement, and that works fine in many situations. If you’re still for long periods, you’re invisible, and the automation assumes the room is empty. The Lafaer LWR02 pairs PIR with 2.4 GHz mmWave radar. The PIR-based motion sees you walking in, and the radar sees the minor stuff, like breathing and shifting on the couch, so the room stays “occupied” for as long as you are in it. The two together also reduce false positives from ceiling fans, curtains, and the dog, because the radar and PIR both must agree before the sensor reports motion.

In Apple Home, that shows up as an occupancy sensor and a motion sensor from the same device.

“Turn on the lights when someone enters” is a common automation I use, but it can be tricky. What if you only want it when it’s not light outside? Doing it based on time of day sometimes works, but what about depending on where the windows are facing, etc.? You might have a room that gets darker an hour earlier than another room. “Turn on the lights when someone enters, and it’s dark in the room” is what the light sensor can handle for you.

In the Home app, that means triggering a sensor for occupancy, then converting the automation into a Shortcut and adding a condition for the light level. It’s a few extra steps, but it does really give you more fine control over how it works.

Presence, motion, light, temperature, and humidity all come from the same device, and each one appears in Apple Home as its own sensor, so you can build automations around whichever ones fit the room.

It’s IPX3-rated, so bathrooms, kitchens, and laundry rooms are fine to use in. Coverage is about 13 feet for presence and 26 for motion across about 120 degrees, which works in a bedroom, office, or bathroom. It’s not going to cover a great room from one corner. The base is a magnetic half sphere, so you can aim it, and it mounts with adhesive or sits on a shelf. I generally like to use the shelf for these types of sensors.

The Lafaer LWR02 is Matter over Thread, so it pairs directly with a HomePod, HomePod mini, or Apple TV 4K with no Lafaer hub or account needed. It runs on two included AAA batteries, is rated for up to two years, and rechargeable AAAs work with it as well. Thread is why a sensor doing this much can last that long on batteries. All sensor data is processed locally, so it only uses a trickle on the batteries.

Lights that turn off while you’re sitting still in the room are the reason a lot of people stop using motion automations in smart homes. The Lafaer LWR02 fixes that with mmWave radar and then lets you have more granular control of light-based automations based on what’s actually in the environment in the room, not just the time of day.

The Lafaer 5-in-1 presence sensor is available on Amazon.
