When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When GTA 6 finally dropped last week after more than a decade of waiting, I knew playing it on a standard TV setup wasn't going to cut it.

Vice City is practically built out of neon sunsets, flashing police strobes, and blinding beachfront sunlight, and I wanted that chaos spilling off the screen and straight onto my living room walls.

That is why I finally set up the Philips Smart LED Screen Sync behind my TV. Built on Philips' more budget-friendly smart lighting line, it is discounted right now for Black Friday — and I know this because I was manning the Amazon live blog when I spotted it.

Even better, the kit bundles both the screen-reading sensor and a four-sided RGBIC lightstrip right in the box.

I finally installed this Philips screen-sync LED strip behind my TV, and it’s a total game-changer. Pairing reactive ambient lighting with GTA 6 right after launch adds a whole new layer of immersion that makes every session feel unreal.

I will admit I was skeptical about how painless the installation would be when all I wanted to do was jump into the game. Fortunately, the whole process took less than ten minutes. You stick the four-sided lightstrip around the back of your TV, perch the compact fisheye camera on top of the bezel, and let the app run an automatic calibration.

It maps the corners of your display on its own, though you can tweak the anchor points manually if your TV sits at an awkward angle. Because it relies on an optical fisheye lens to read the screen in real time rather than intercepting an HDMI signal, there is also zero input lag added to your console and no need to worry about bandwidth bottlenecks.

The WiZ app is where you can customise how it looks. I found after having a play around that Vibrant mode is my personal favorite, especially once you nudge the Saturation and Intensity sliders up so the colors really pop.

When they first lit up, electric pink and cyan neon signs bled softly out from the left edge of the frame while warm, syrupy golden-hour skies glow across the top, wrapping your whole field of vision in atmosphere. Everything you're playing, suddenly, feels so much more real.

Beyond looking incredible, that responsive halo actually cut down on my eye strain. I tend to game late into the night and already suffer from dry eyes, so the contrast of a bright screen in a dark room normally wears me out pretty fast. I didn't have any of that once I set these up, though, as the glow softens the glare and gives my eyes a break.

Is a camera mounted on top of your TV slightly less sleek than a hidden HDMI box? Sure. Does a dark room keep the color tracking noticeably more accurate than broad daylight? Definitely. Yet it completely changes how a game feels (and don't even get me started on how good it makes movies look!)

Throw in the fact that it is marked down right now for Black Friday, and it is hands down one of the best TV upgrades you can make.

#3259. MS NOW Hosts Sign On To Letter Urging Adoption Of “Fair” WGAE Contract; Network Says Talks Are Ongoing And “Constructive”

The Writers Guild of America, East said that a number of MS NOW hosts — including Rachel Maddow, Jen Psaki, Chris Hayes and Nicolle Wallace — have signed on to a letter of solidarity urging the network to adopt a new contract that expands representation and boosts annual and minimum wage increases to keep pace with inflation.

The network, meanwhile, says that talks have progressed and have been “constructive,” while stating that it supports employees’ right to organize. But it has contended that proposed wage increases would be out of line with what other employees across the company and at other networks have received. Related Stories News Joe Rogan's The Most Trusted Name In Media For Dudes - Especially Dudes With Daddy Issues News Skydance Buyouts Impact CBS Stations; Local Chicago Anchor Among Those Departing

The WGAE represents about 300 members, and, per the union, is looking for recognition of 50 additional employees in digital, audio and longform, newsgathering, planning and the DC bureau. Watch on Deadline

“As hosts and guests of MS NOW programs, we stand in solidarity with the MS NOW Union as they fight for a contract that addresses inflation, AI protections, and retirement security. As one of the most trusted names in news, we are proud of our programming and the MS NOW producers that make it possible,” the letter stated.

“We’re disappointed that Versant Media’s decision makers expect unit members to work extra hours creating new digital content, without treating it as extra work or paying for it. On top of that, we are disappointed that Versant Media will not agree to the Union’s demands for annual and minimum wage increases that keep pace with inflation,” the letter added.

Other on-air figures who signed the letter include Ali Velshi, Amy McGrath, Alicia Menendez, Jacob Soboroff, David Noriega, Jillian Frankel, Ayman Mohyeldin, Katie Phang, Christine Jansing, Symone Sanders Townsend, Antonia Hylton, Jonathan Capehart and Michael Steele.

Rebecca Kutler, the president of MS NOW, wrote in a memo to employees, “Let me be clear: we support our employees’ right to organize, to be represented, and to advocate for themselves. That has never been in question, nor should it be.”

She noted that the WGAE had reached agreement with other labor unions including IATSE and the DGA, and that they have already reached tentative agreements on a number of issues with the WGAE and have “shown a willingness to find common ground where differences remain.”

“We offer the highest starting salaries among our peers, having raised entry-level salaries significantly over the last five years, and the starting point for each role’s salary range is typically higher than our broadcast and cable news competitors,” she wrote.

She also cited the network’s hiring for more than 200 positions over the past year, as other newsrooms cut back. MS NOW has been building its newsgathering operation since the split from Comcast meant that NBC News was no longer a sister network.

The first contract for the MS NOW Union [previously MSNBC] was reached in 2023 and included a 3% pay increase for every year of the agreement’s duration. It also included “vital improvements to policies regarding extra pay for additional work, overnight work, and out-of-title work,” per the WGAE.

According to the network, they have offered guaranteed 3% salary increases, enhanced pay for filling in at an upgraded position, and a 33% increase in the night shift allowance per shift for exempt employees, crediting on-call time as time worked, as well as AI-related protections, among other proposals.

Per the network, WGAE is seeking 5% annual wage increases over the next two years and a 4.5% increase in the third year, as well as a 4% increase in salary minimums at signing and another 4.5% increase in 2029.

Kutler wrote that the network’s audience growth “does not insulate us from the financial pressures reshaping our industry. It takes a realistic understanding of these market pressures for us to continue our success.”

The letters from the WGAE and Kutler are below:

As hosts and guests of MS NOW programs, we stand in solidarity with the MS NOW Union as they fight for a contract that addresses inflation, AI protections, and retirement security. As one of the most trusted names in news, we are proud of our programming and the MS NOW producers that make it possible.We’re disappointed that Versant Media’s decision makers expect unit members to work extra hours creating new digital content, without treating it as extra work or paying for it. On top of that, we are disappointed that Versant Media will not agree to the Union’s demands for annual and minimum wage increases that keep pace with inflation.We are calling on the Company to agree to a quick and fair process to recognize all employees’ rightful place in the MS NOW Union without division or delay. Additionally, we call on the Company to agree to a contract that will protect wages, benefits, and security at work.

Team,As we continue to negotiate with the Writers Guild of America East, I’d like to give you an update about where we stand.For those unfamiliar with this process, the WGAE represents a group of our editorial employees in a collective bargaining unit that negotiates their compensation and other terms of employment. We reached an initial agreement with this union in 2023, and now that contract is set to expire on Dec. 3.Let me be clear: we support our employees’ right to organize, to be represented, and to advocate for themselves. That has never been in question, nor should it be. In the past year, we have successfully reached new collective bargaining agreements with other labor organizations, including two International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees locals and the Directors Guild of America, and have approached these negotiations with the same mindset. We have already reached tentative agreements with WGAE on numerous issues throughout this process and shown a willingness to find common ground where differences remain. We have made meaningful proposals to increase compensation, address workload concerns, expand opportunities for growth and advancement, and provide protections against AI, among many other offerings.We offer the highest starting salaries among our peers, having raised entry-level salaries significantly over the last five years, and the starting point for each role’s salary range is typically higher than our broadcast and cable news competitors. We are a workforce that is embracing new technologies and creating opportunities for employees to broaden their skill sets and advance their careers. Our goal is to ensure our employees will grow alongside our business and the broader industry. These commitments are part of the reason we have a company-wide attrition rate well below national averages. Plus, while many other news organizations are cutting back their newsrooms and trimming roles, we have filled more than 200 in the past year at MS NOW and continue recruiting for dozens of open positions.We are enormously proud of MS NOW’s performance; our strong audience metrics are a testament to the work you do every day. But this success does not insulate us from the financial pressures reshaping our industry. It takes a realistic understanding of these market pressures for us to continue our success. We must weigh every financial commitment against our ability to invest in journalism, develop new programming, hire journalists, cover the 2028 presidential campaign, and build out platforms that will carry MS NOW into the future, including our direct-to-consumer offering.We will continue to compensate our employees fairly and competitively, while protecting our long-term growth. Those responsibilities are not mutually exclusive, but they require thoughtful decisions.As we approach the final weeks of these negotiations, let’s stay focused on what unites us: our shared commitment to the journalism we produce, the audiences who count on us, and the future of MS NOW. I am optimistic that together we will reach a fair and responsible agreement that reflects the respect we have for our colleagues and the work we do together.If you have any questions, please don’t hesitate to reach out to me, Greg, Madeleine, Scott, Marcus, or anyone on our leadership team. Our doors are always open.Rebecca

#3258. The Best Gifts for Every Tech Nerd in Your Life

This series will help you pick the perfect presents, decor, and activities to make this Christmas the Best Christmas Ever.

Our grandparents could drop some treats in a sock and call it Christmas, secure in the knowledge that their children would be delighted by an orange. These days, though, everyone from your tech-obsessed granny to your cutting-edge teen wants to be impressed. Luckily, there's a mind-blowing high-tech gadget out there for everyone.

I don't know anyone who wouldn't appreciate finding these display glasses in their Christmas stocking. The Xbx a01s are sunglasses you can plug into any device with a USB-C port to create your own personal, private monitor. The resulting picture is the equivalent of a 142" TV. The refresh rate is a crisp 120Hz, and the glasses support HDR10 and real-time SDR-to-HDR upscaling and billions of colors, all in a package that weighs only 62 grams. In other words: It's an HD TV you can carry in your pocket and wear on your face. The $299 list price won't break your wallet either. They're the best smart glasses for most people. Check out my full review for more details.

It can be hard to buy a gift for a health-focused person. They usually don't want booze and they like putting in effort. But the Whoop Peak 5 fitness tracker will brighten the Christmas morning of the most diehard athlete. It's more versatile than a watch (you can wear it on your bicep and even in your underwear) and it monitors heart rate, respiratory rate, heart rate variability, skin temperature, blood oxygen levels, daily activity, and sleep—basically everything I don't worry about. Check out Lifehacker's senior health editor Beth Skwarecki's in-depth look at the Whoop Peak 5 for more details.

You cannot go wrong with a GoPro. The company's easy-to-use, hard-to-break cameras are synonymous with "action photography" and compact enough to fit in a stocking. If there's a snowboarder, skateboarder, kayaker, or BMX racer on your list, this is a must. Even if your giftee isn't an adventurer, the GoPro Hero 13 supports additional lenses and filters that let users go beyond the "gnarly fish-eye, dude" photography and videography of past generations. Check out associate tech editor Michelle Ehrhardt's GoPro Hero 13 review for more details.

Everyone wants their own droid. Beni from Mondo Robotics is a camera robot that takes 4K video while autonomously following its subject wherever they go. If you want to get action footage, there's no need to hassle with a tripod or another person: You can control Beni with the remote, or simply tell it to follow you. It can be set to track you from behind, from the side, or it can circle you, and you can adjust what it is doing from the app or remote on the fly, so there's no limit to the kind of elaborate shots it can pull off. Plus it's freakin' adorable. The $799 list price might be a bit steep for most gift-givers, but as far as how well it works and how much fun I've had using it, it's worth the money.

The R36 Max 2 retro handheld game console lets you take your gaming anywhere. It comes with over 20,000 games pre-installed, so you can play every title from classic consoles like the Atari 2600 or the PlayStation 1, as well as just about every arcade game anyone ever dropped a coin into, all for less than $100. I paid more than that in quarters just to beat Dragon's Lair!

I'm obsessed with the Yamaha Seqtrak. It crams a drum machine, sequencer, sampler, three separate synthesizers, and a speaker into a package small enough to put into a Christmas stocking. It's a complete mobile studio—everything you need to produce a song or beat—but it also integrates with your computer's DAW and other MIDI gear to become part of your home studio. All that for only $300!

The Flipper Zero is a must-have device for the hardcore, glasses-wearing, circuit-bender type of techie. Its ability to do evil deeds like hack ATMs is greatly exaggerated, but the Flipper is still a technological Swiss Army knife that lets you read and manipulate the invisible waves around you, from radio waves to RFID, NFC, Bluetooth, and wifi signals. It's educational, fascinating, and powerful; how you use that power is your business.

If you're giving a gift to a would-be Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, this miniature, wireless microscope will rock their holiday. It's easy to set up, works with PCs, Android, or iOS devices, magnifies things up to 1000x, and takes 1080p pictures of your discoveries.

#3257. AirPods 5 vs AirPods Pro 3: Which should you buy this holiday season?

The holiday shopping season is here, and Apple’s AirPods are sure to be one of the most popular gifts. If you’re shopping for AirPods, Apple sells three different models: AirPods 5, AirPods Pro 3, and AirPods Max 2. Here’s how they compare.

AirPods 5 were introduced in September and come in two different versions. Unlike their predecessors, both versions of AirPods 5 offer Active Noise Cancellation. They differ in the charging case, battery life, and volume control. The base model AirPods 5 ($129) come with a case that can only charge via USB-C.

The case for the higher-end AirPods 5 ($149) supports wireless charging and Find My. You also get one extra hour of battery life. The higher-end model also adds on-stem volume control, so you can adjust the volume just by swiping up or down on one of the earbud stems.

Here’s a full comparison between both AirPods 5 models:

The key thing about AirPods 5 is their open-ear design, unlike the in-ear design of the AirPods Pro 3 (more on those later). Even with that open-ear design, AirPods 5 offer incredible Active Noise Cancellation capabilities.

If you are shopping for AirPods 5, I do recommend spending the extra $20 to get the higher-end model. The better charging case alone is worth the extra money. With Find My integration and a built-in speaker, you can track your AirPods and play a sound from the case if you lose them.

If the person you’re shopping for doesn’t like in-ear earbuds, AirPods 5 are an excellent choice.

For most people, though, AirPods Pro 3 are probably the better choice …

AirPods Pro 3 are Apple’s most capable earbuds, even with the introduction of AirPods 5 this year. They offer an in-ear fit and come with five foam-infused silicone ear tip sizes. With that in-ear design, AirPods Pro 3 can offer up to 3x stronger noise cancellation than AirPods 5. In my testing, this difference is notable.

AirPods Pro 3 also offer several other features you won’t find on AirPods 5, including a heart rate sensor for workouts, plus Hearing Test, Hearing Aid, and Hearing Protection features.

I still think AirPods Pro 3 are one of the best products in Apple’s lineup today. I wear mine for multiple hours every single day and can’t imagine life without them. I love the in-ear fit, and the ANC still impresses me, whether I’m at home or somewhere like a coffee shop.

If you know the person you’re shopping for (whether it’s yourself or someone else) likes the in-ear earbud design, I think AirPods Pro 3 are the best option. This is especially true when AirPods Pro 3 are on sale, like they are right now at $149. The price difference between AirPods 5 and AirPods Pro 3 is very small, and you’re getting a much better product.

Finally, we have AirPods Max. These are Apple’s only option for people who want AirPods in an over-ear headphone form factor. Last year, they were pretty hard to recommend since they’d gone five years without a real upgrade.

This year, however, Apple officially introduced AirPods Max 2, bringing modern features to Apple’s high-end headphones. This includes features like Adaptive Audio, Conversation Awareness, Personalized Volume, and more.

AirPods Max 2 are a far more compelling option than AirPods Max were at this time last year. They’re still pricey, but I love the aesthetics and find them very comfortable. There’s something about the premium aluminum design with an elegant Digital Crown that really stands out.

If you’re looking to splurge this holiday season, AirPods Max 2 are a great choice. For more realistic budgets, I think AirPods Pro 3 are the best option.

Are you planning to buy anyone AirPods this holiday season? Are they on your wishlist? Let us know down in the comments.

#3256. Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

The AI pioneer says it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big issues

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

Andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he says he has identified the next big shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

Ng’s current efforts are focused on his company Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he says can yield “small data” solutions to big issues in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

The great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

Andrew Ng: This is a big question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having said that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

Ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a new paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

Ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

Having said that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of users, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing company with millions of users.

Ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

“In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI

I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and said, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

Over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing new here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

Ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and said, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

The data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one company or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that showed up.

You often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

Ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

When you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand new model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

Ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having said that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For big data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng

For example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very quickly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

Ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. New tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an important piece of the puzzle.

One of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

Ng: In AI, data cleaning is important, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention quickly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

For example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

Ng: I think synthetic data is an important tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

Ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

“In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng

Synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

To make these issues more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a company approaches Landing AI and says it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

Ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

One of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

How do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

Ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift issue. I find it really important to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and update the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

Ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent new neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s important for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

Ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print issue as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”

Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor, where she helps develop and shape the magazine’s longform stories. She also oversees Spectrum's coverage of artificial intelligence and biomedical engineering. She holds a master’s degree in journalism from Columbia University.

#3255. Kevin Kline Joins Meryl Streep In Netflix’s ‘The Corrections’

Academy Award winner Kevin Kline is set to star opposite the previously announced Meryl Streep in The Corrections, Netflix‘s series adaptation of Jonathan Franzen’s National Book Award winner from Paramount Television Studios.

Kline plays Alfred Lambert, the husband of Streep’s Enid Lambert. A once-powerful patriarch battling the afflictions of aging, Alfred is a man of strict principles and old-fashioned decorum who must come to terms with his three very modern children — a daughter whose secrets he can no longer protect, an older son who has displaced him as the authority in the family, and a wayward son whose forgiveness he yearns for. Related Stories News Netflix Dates Jamie Foxx's Olympic Boxing Drama 'Fight For '84' News 'The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey': Melissa McCarthy & Clive Owen Play Grieving, Overly Scrutinized Parents In Trailer For Netflix Series

The series brings Kline and Streep back together more than 40 years after they first collaborated on Sophie’s Choice, the Academy Award-winning classic which marked Kline’s feature film debut. Over the years, the duo have also worked together on the films A Prairie Home Companion and Ricki and the Flash, along with a handful of stage productions. Watch on Deadline

The Corrections is a comic portrait of a Midwestern family whose three unmoored adult siblings desperately resist their mother’s wish for one last Christmas together — each undone by the delusional ambitions that were supposed to save them from becoming their parents.

Franzen adapted his book for Netflix and exec produces the limited drama alongside American Fiction‘s Cord Jefferson, who also directs all episodes. Other exec producers include Mark Roybal (Task, Mare of Easttown) and Paul Lee (Task, The Summer I Turned Pretty) for wiip; Nicole Clemens (Sexy Beast, Shantaram); Amy Sayres and Streep.

An Oscar and three-time Tony Award winner, Kline is best known for turns in such classic films as A Fish Called Wanda, Sophie’s Choice and The Big Chill. Most recently, he’s been seen starring in MGM+’s American Classic, opposite Laura Linney, and Alfonso Cuarón’s Emmy-nominated Apple series Disclaimer, opposite Cate Blanchett and Sacha Baron Cohen. He is repped by UTA and Berwick & Kovacik.

#3254. 10 Hacks Every 'GTA 6' Player Should Know

I've been playing Grand Theft Auto VI since launch, and I'm having a blast so far. The world feels even more detailed and immersive than previous GTA games, which means there's a lot to learn beyond the basic tutorials and prompts the game shares at the beginning. These are the 10 GTA 6 hacks I used to improve the game's quality of life. If you do the same, you'll spend more time immersed in the world, and less time fighting the game's default settings.

I'm not going to share any spoilers here, but you should know that the side quests in Chapter 1 are important. If you ignore all the optional quests or small asks by other characters, you won't be able to return to those later. These are small things like fixing up the house for Lucia, meditating with her, and buying her a necklace when she asks you to. All of these have an impact on your progress. Take your time in this chapter, and remember to save before starting the mission called "Recalibration." That mission leads to Tourist Trap, which is the point of no return for Chapter 1.

If you're used to playing racing games, you'll find the driving experience in GTA VI to be quite different. It's hard to keep an eye on minimap directions while you're also getting used to vehicles in the game, and I used voice navigation to ensure that I don't keep getting lost, particularly for time-sensitive missions. You can enable this by going to GTA VI settings > Audio > GPS Voice > Voice. If you're playing the game on PS5, your DualSense controller's speaker plays GPS voice prompts. This is great as those alerts can be hard to hear over all other in-game sounds from your TV's speaker.

Using GTA 6's default controls, making Jason and Lucia run is quite annoying. The game makes you hold L3 to run, which hurts my thumbs. If you alter movement speed in settings, you can make the characters run just by using the left stick. You can walk by easing off the left stick, or switch to a fast walk, jog, or run when you push the stick all the way. Tweak this by going to GTA VI settings > Gameplay > Movement Speed > Jog. This lets you move faster without draining your stamina. You can also change from Jog to Run if you want the fastest possible movement speed with the left stick. Having said that, my pro tip is to go to Control Scheme in settings, and switch to Classic. This lets you run by holding the X button, as opposed to L3 with default controls.

Haptic strength is one area where GTA 6 takes the immersion a bit too far, as it's dialed up to the maximum level by default. This makes the controller's vibration strength a bit too intense for my liking, and also has a negative impact on battery life. You can fix that by reducing haptic strength a little. It's under GTA VI settings > Controller > Vibration & Haptics Strength.

Many modern controllers develop "stick drift," an issue where small movements of the analog sticks register as large inputs. This causes a big problem in games that require precise inputs, such as GTA 6. To counter this potential problem, the game allows you to adjust the deadzone for each analog stick in your controller. That said, this setting can be used to your advantage, even if you don't have stick drift issues in your controller. I recommend dialing up the deadzone to 7 to improve the driving experience. I find most cars in GTA 6 to be a bit floaty to drive, and adjusting the deadzone fixes this issue to a large extent.

Committing a heist attracts heat in GTA 6, and there are many different ways to escape the attention of in-game cops. The usual tricks include stocking up on outfits to change into, parking your vehicle a block or two away, and being so stealthy that you leave no witnesses to your crimes. However, an underrated trick involves using the pickup truck you get at the start of the game. Get a bike in the game, and stash it in your pickup truck. Then, use the truck to drive to the crime scene, and hide the truck a short distance away. Unload the bike, and use it to get to the crime scene. Once the heist is complete, ditch the bike, and run to your truck. Witnesses won't have seen you using the truck, which allows you to escape the area quickly.

If you are using a car as a getaway vehicle, you can use two tricks to make a smooth escape. First, double-tap the Triangle button to exit your vehicle without switching off its engine. When you return to the vehicle in a hurry, you can escape a lot faster. If you have quick fingers, you can double-tap Triangle first, and just as your character is about to exit the vehicle, press L3 (or X, if you use classic controls). This leaves the car's door open, and saves you a little more time when you're fleeing.

I suffer from chronic migraines, and I am sensitive to bright lights. Fortunately, GTA 6 has a bunch of accessibility settings that help me play the game for longer. Even if you don't face the same issues, these settings will help reduce eye strain in longer play sessions. Go to GTA VI settings > Display > Flashbang, and switch to Dark. This stops flashbangs from showing a bright white light when they go off. On the same settings page, you can tweak Player Status Effects Intensity to reduce screen effects when your character is low on health or stamina. You can also enable Brightness Reduction to reduce the intensity of bright lights in the game, and try Focus Trail Colorblind Mode if you find it hard to distinguish between different colors.

I haven't been able to play first-person shooters for decades because the camera movement makes me nauseous and gives me a headache. Of late, I've noticed that it's getting harder to play third-person games too. My first two hours in GTA 6 had me quite worried because I was feeling quite sick, and I had to turn off my PS5. Luckily for me, I found a few tweaks to mitigate this problem. You can do that in GTA VI settings > UI > Persistent Center Dot. This permanently shows a white dot in the center of the screen, and it reduced my motion sickness enough to help me play the game. You can also go to GTA VI settings > Camera, reduce Camera Bob, and turn off Camera Shake, and Weapon Sway. I also recommend going to the Controller tab in settings, and tweaking all the options under Aim & Look Sensitivity until you find a comfortable level.

GTA 6 includes realistic ringing sounds that linger after explosions in the game. This may be fine for some people, but it can negatively affect some players' gaming sessions. Those who suffer from tinnitus or chronic migraines may not enjoy those ringing sounds, and, luckily, the game allows you to disable them. Open GTA 6's in-game settings, and enable the feature from Audio > Tinnitus Reduction.

These five Prime Video movies deserve a spot on your Christmas watchlist

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Christmas is not too far away, which means it’s the perfect time to start working your way through some festive movies. The season has already begun for me, and I always love having a Christmas movie playing in the background while I get on with things. Thankfully, you don’t have to look far for something to watch, as Prime Video has plenty of holiday treats worth adding to your watchlist.

Whether you’re in the mood for a feel-good romantic comedy, a laugh-out-loud festive adventure or a classic Christmas favorite, there’s something for every kind of movie night. I’ve rounded up five of the best Christmas movies to stream on Prime Video right now, including a few familiar gems and some newer releases you might have missed.

So grab a blanket, make yourself a hot chocolate and settle in for a little holiday movie marathon.

Of course, we had to start with one of the most iconic Christmas movies of all time. “Elf” has become a modern holiday staple, and a big part of its charm comes from Jon Favreau and Will Ferrell’s approach to the comedy. The film holds a real nostalgic festive look and includes plenty of cozy moments and wonderfully silly humor. Favreau also recognized the value of letting improvised scenes breathe, including Buddy’s hilarious deadpan exchange with a colleague in the office mailroom. It's the contrast between Buddy’s childlike enthusiasm and everyone else’s everyday cynicism that makes the comedy work so well.

After accidentally crawling into Santa’s sack as a baby, Buddy (Will Ferrell) is transported to the North Pole, where he’s raised by Santa’s elves. However, after discovering he’s actually human, the adult Buddy sets off for New York City to find his biological father, Walter Hobbs (James Caan), a workaholic children’s book publisher who has no idea he exists. Wearing his full elf outfit, Buddy struggles to fit into the busy city while getting to know his new family, including his younger half-brother Michael (Daniel Tay). Along the way, he also catches the attention of department-store employee Jovie (Zooey Deschanel).

“Scrooged” is a great choice if you prefer your Christmas movies with a slightly darker edge. Starring Bill Murray, this modern take on Charles Dickens’ “A Christmas Carol” swaps traditional festive sweetness for sharp comedy, media satire and plenty of cynical laughs. It might have divided audiences when it first arrived, but it’s since become a cult Christmas favorite, and definitely one I add to my watchlist this time of year. I also appreciate how it balances its darker comedy with some genuinely heartfelt moments. Think of it as the perfect anti-Hallmark holiday movie.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Frank Cross (Bill Murray) is a ruthless and cynical television executive preparing a lavish live broadcast of Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol on Christmas Eve. More interested in ratings than giving his employees time off, Frank has little patience for anyone who gets in his way. But his plans are interrupted when the ghost of his former mentor appears, warning him that three spirits will soon pay him a visit. Over the course of the night, the Ghosts of Christmas Past, Present and Future take Frank on a series of unexpected journeys, forcing him to confront his childhood, his relationships and what lies ahead if he continues down his current path.

“Red One” might have divided critics, but there’s plenty of festive fun to be had in this big-budget Christmas action-comedy. Dwayne Johnson and Chris Evans make an entertaining double act, with their buddy-comedy chemistry helping the film through some of its cheesier moments. J.K. Simmons is another highlight as a surprisingly buff and wonderfully enthusiastic Santa Claus. It’s not exactly subtle, but I found it an enjoyable seasonal watch, especially if you like a generous dose of action and silliness in Christmas flicks.

When Santa Claus (J.K. Simmons), also known by his codename Red One, is kidnapped from the North Pole just days before Christmas, it’s up to his head of security, Callum Drift (Dwayne Johnson), to bring him home. With Christmas Eve fast approaching, Callum reluctantly joins forces with Jack O’Malley (Chris Evans), a notorious bounty hunter and hacker whose actions inadvertently exposed Santa’s secret location. Together, the unlikely pair embark on a globe-trotting rescue mission, travelling across the world and encountering all sorts of mythical creatures along the way.

It’s interesting to think that “It’s a Wonderful Life” wasn’t originally intended to become a Christmas movie. After its copyright wasn’t renewed in 1974, it became a regular fixture on television during the festive season, introducing new generations to Frank Capra’s classic. And it’s easy to see why it stuck around. James Stewart delivers a wonderful performance in a story that reminds us there’s always hope, even during the darkest times. It’s one of those genuinely feel-good films that leaves you feeling a little more positive about life.

George Bailey (James Stewart) is a businessman living in the small town of Bedford Falls who has spent much of his life putting his own ambitions aside to help others. But when a financial crisis threatens his family business on Christmas Eve, George finds himself facing the possibility of losing everything. Overwhelmed by his circumstances, he begins to question what the world would look like if he had never been born. That’s when Clarence, a guardian angel hoping to earn his wings, arrives to show George an alternate version of Bedford Falls, where he discovers just how differently things might have turned out without him.

It’s also that time of year when streaming services start rolling out their festive originals, and Prime Video is getting into the Christmas spirit with “Clashing Through the Snow.” Starring Christopher Briney from “The Summer I Turned Pretty” and Michelle Randolph, this cozy romantic comedy has all the ingredients for an enjoyable holiday watch. It has the classic enemies-to-lovers setup, which gives the central relationship plenty of room for bickering and romantic tension. Add in a snowy road trip and two appealing leads, and there’s plenty to enjoy. The timing is also spot on, arriving just as Thanksgiving week kicks off.

In “Clashing Through the Snow,” rival publishing editors Ryan Mitchell (Christopher Briney) and Hannah Hendricks (Michelle Randolph) find themselves competing for their jobs after their company announces budget cuts. Both are sent to New York to secure a major book deal that could save their careers, but their plans take a turn when a Christmas snowstorm grounds their flight. With no other way to reach the city in time, the pair are forced to share a rental car and embark on a cross-country road trip together. Along the way, unexpected detours, roadside mishaps and encounters with strangers make their journey far more complicated than either anticipated.

Alix is a Senior Streaming Writer at Tom’s Guide, which basically means watching the best movies and TV shows and then writing about them. It’s a dream job for someone who’s been obsessed with storytelling since she first figured out how to work a remote.

Before joining Tom’s Guide, Alix honed her skills as a staff writer with outlets like Screen Rant and Bough Digital, where she discovered her love for the entertainment industry.

She heads to the cinema every week as a tradition, no matter what’s showing. For her, movies aren’t just entertainment — they’re a ritual, a comfort, and a constant source of inspiration. When she’s not at her desk or at the cinema, you’ll probably find her deep into a horror video game on her PC.

#3251. Consumer Appetite for Personal AI Goes Mainstream

Nearly 70 percent of respondents say they want an AI assistant in their next device, according to a new report

Qualcomm builds intelligent, connected, computing and AI solutions that transform industries and advance human progress.

A recent report by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide, shows that around 70 percent of respondents express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.

This article is brought to you by Qualcomm Technologies.

For many consumers, much of the promise and appeal of AI is personal. Consumers are looking past generic tools and want to know how these technologies will help them in their daily lives. These trends coincide with the advent of new classes of wearable devices that, in addition to being able to leverage powerful frontier models, feature built-in intelligence that understand the context of a user. Where are they? What are they seeing and hearing? What are their habits, their preferences, their schedules?

It’s an astonishing pivot, from passive accessories that served mostly to send users smartphone notifications to proactive, intelligent companions. The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI. And it shifts the focus toward you, the user.

These new technologies are exciting. But what do consumers really want?

A Personal AI report, commissioned by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide (the U.S., U.K., Germany, India, Brazil, and China) focused on the rise of personal AI in intelligent wearables looks deeply at these developments.

The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI.

Survey respondents are less interested in single devices and are responding more to the idea of connected ecosystems. As people expand their roster of devices, it only makes sense. Instead of relying entirely on a smartphone and a laptop, respondents also have connected technology in their cars, as well as intelligent wearables like smartwatches, smart glasses, hearables, and other wearables like rings, pins, and pendants. They want those devices to work in concert, and the way to do that is to decentralize any single one of them. Instead, the AI agent that knows the user and works across all of those devices becomes the unifying factor.

Consider a typical workday: A user’s watch detects it is time to leave for a meeting and, with permission, their AI agent factors in calendar details, real-time traffic and battery status across their devices. In the car, it suggests the best route and briefs them on their meeting agenda. As they arrive, smart glasses surface a discreet reminder, such as the meeting location or the name of a new contact, while the phone stays in their pocket. No one device has to do everything; each plays the role it is best suited for, coordinated by a personal AI agent that understands the user’s context and acts only at the user’s direction.

With this in mind, simply adding more hardware to the mix isn’t sufficient. Even though respondents will be open to new form factors, they’ll demand more from their ecosystem of devices. They’ll be sensitive to points of friction and needless complexity, and they’ll require each new device to bring something new to the table — “incremental intelligence, convenience, or contextual awareness that their existing devices cannot deliver on their own what the report,” reads the report.

The usage trends are up. The report found that those who own wearables are already using AI frequently (60 percent use it at least weekly), which indicates that it’s becoming less of a fun experiment for early adopters and more of a critical mass habit.

The “always-on” nature of intelligent wearables appears to be winning respondents, too. The report found the following statistics on average continuous wear among users:

But for all the excitement and engagement around intelligent wearables, there’s a gating factor: trust. As use cases for intelligent wearables expands to more personal and persistent experiences, trust is a necessity for Personal AI.

Notably, the report found that respondents expressed more interest in adopting intelligent wearables when Snapdragon was introduced as the enabling platform. This reinforces the value of having an established, trusted technology foundation in the mix.

The report shows that consumer appetite for AI is high, with 60-70 percent of those surveyed expressing interest in advanced AI as they consider a new device. That’s a constant. But remaining purchase drivers differed between device categories.

Audio playback quality is the most influential purchase driver for true wireless earbuds and headphones. For smartwatches, it’s display quality and responsiveness. Respondents are less concerned about technical specifications than aesthetics like materials and finish when it comes to devices like smart rings and pendants. And for smart glasses, it’s all about the type of control, whether it’s voice, gesture, or touch.

Artificial intelligence is entering a new phase, one that is deeply personal, continuously present, and seamlessly embedded into the devices we wear every day. This evolution, which we define as “Personal AI”, represents a shift away from generic, cloud-only intelligence toward AI that understands individuals in context: their habits, preferences, environments, and intent, in real time.

Alongside these purchase drivers is another key finding: Consumer appetite for Personal AI agents has gone mainstream. The report says that 70 percent of respondents “express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.” With each individual as the center of their own ecosystem, voice becomes the most critical, natural method for interacting with agents.

Intelligent wearables comprise much of the hardware of this “ecosystem of you.” Consumers are interested in ecosystems instead of single devices, and they’re looking for agentic AI capabilities that understand and act on their behalf.

Yet so much of the industry remains undefined. OEMs and technology makers have an enormous opportunity right now to innovate and iterate on the strong technological foundations that platform makers are building. And the roadmap for what consumers want is clear.

All percentages, consumer behaviors, and attitudes stated in this report are based only on the responses of the individuals who participated in our survey.

Qualcomm Technologies is a global leader in communications and computing technologies, including leading-edge AI, high-performance, low-power computing, and connectivity solutions. Headquartered in San Diego, Calif., the company develops technologies for next-generation mobile networks and smart devices, and designs semiconductors such as mobile processors and AI chips.

The bias is deafening. Qualcomm, a chip manufacturer that is all in on AI, makes a survey and then states they found everyone loves using AI, the very AI that will run on Qualcomm chips. Clearly they don't have a conflict of interest in this. /s

EXCLUSIVE: Theatrical tech, distribution and management corp Qube Cinema has hired Imax and 20th Century Fox distribution vet Craig Dehmel as their new Head of Studio Relations.

Dehmel will be based in Los Angeles for Qube Wire, which has a global content distribution service which connects with over 7,000 theaters worldwide. In his new position, Dehmel will lead strategic customer development and strengthen senior-level relationships across Hollywood studios, independent distributors, and content owners.

Dehmel’s 35 years in the motion picture industry includes serving as Head of Global Distribution at Imax, where he led the planning, programming, and distribution of Hollywood studio, local-language, documentary, and special-content releases across more than 1,700 Imax screens worldwide. Related Stories Sports Imax To Screen Super Bowl In Deal With Disney, NFL News Imax Inks Largest UK Deal With Cinema Chain Acquired By Former Cineworld CEO Mooky Greidinger

Prior to Imax, Dehmel spent 16 years at 20th Century Fox, where he held senior roles in sales, strategic planning, and international distribution, culminating in his appointment as EVP, InternationalDistribution. He is a member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts & Sciences, serving in its Executive Branch, and has been a guest lecturer at the UCLA Anderson School of Management for more than two decades. Watch on Deadline

“Qube Wire’s growth reflects the confidence that studios, distributors, and exhibitors place in our technology and services. As our global network continues to expand, strengthening our relationships with content owners and studio partners is central to our plans,” said Harsh Rohatgi, CEO of Qube Cinema.

“Craig brings an exceptional understanding of the global theatrical business and longstandingrelationships across the industry. #3248. Multiphysics Modeling for Next-Generation Electromagnetic Manufacturing Technologies



Advances in sensing, manufacturing, computational resources, and data-driven methods are enabling new approaches to electromagnetic sensing, non-destructive evaluation, and advanced materials processing. This webinar will demonstrate how the COMSOL Multiphysics software supports predictive modeling by coupling electromagnetic fields with thermal, chemical, mechanical, and transport phenomena across multiple length and time scales.

The first application we will show focuses on eddy-current thermometry for reconstructing three-dimensional temperature fields in metal plates. Temperature-dependent electrical conductivity alters induced currents and magnetic fields, enabling volumetric thermal inference. COMSOL simulations of defects and laser-induced transient heating will support validation of reconstruction algorithms. Multifrequency excitation will be investigated to improve depth discrimination through frequency-dependent penetration depths and sensitivities.

The second application examines microwave-enabled volumetric additive manufacturing of ceramic components. A high-power microwave beamforming array delivers localized energy into three-dimensional volumes, enabling processing of opaque, particle-laden resins. Coupled COMSOL models of electromagnetic propagation, microwave absorption, heat transfer, and ceramic sintering kinetics are used to predict temperature evolution, reaction progression, spatial resolution, and processing scalability. Future extensions will incorporate pulsed excitation, fluid flow, resin viscosity, convection, shrinkage, and solid mechanics.

Together, these examples demonstrate how the COMSOL software can integrate multiphysics modeling with sensing, manufacturing, and data inversion. This webinar will present two applications of coupled electromagnetic and thermal modeling in COMSOL Multiphysics: eddy-current thermometry in metal plates and microwave-assisted processing of ceramic-loaded resins. By connecting simulation with practical engineering systems, COMSOL-based modeling can accelerate technology development, reduce experimental iteration, and support reliable scale-up of next-generation electromagnetic technologies.

#3247. Apple's AirPods Pro 3 Are $100 Off Ahead of Black Friday

Apple AirPods Pro 3 are not only my favorite earbuds I've ever owned, they might also be my favorite headphones of all time. The Pros sound great, come with excellent noise cancellation and transparency modes, and are packed with modern features that go beyond listening to music. I'd recommend these to any Apple user looking for the best overall audio experience at full price, but when they're $100 off, I actively encourage you to buy these now.

On the surface, Apple's third-generation AirPods Pro are among the best ways to listen to audio on your Apple devices. The earbuds sound great: I'm not an audiophile or a headphone reviewer, but to my ears, the Pros deliver excellent sound quality, with plenty of bass and great sound separation. I frequently turn to mine when I want to pay close attention to a new album, or watch a show or movie with intricate sound design. Plus, like other AirPods, the Pros are great for jumping between your various Apple devices. I'm constantly switching between my iPhone, Mac, and Apple TV with mine, and they seamlessly move between each—at least, most of the time.

The noise cancellation on these AirPods is also stellar. I used to take my AirPods Max with me on planes, but lately, I've been fine with just my Pros, since the noise cancellation seemingly blocks just about as much background sound as my over-the-ear headphones. Equally great are both the transparency modes, which pump in outside sounds while you're wearing your AirPods, and Adaptive Transparency, which automatically adjusts the level of transparency based on how loud or soft your surroundings are. This is a great mode for wearing your AirPods in loud environments, so you can still hear everything without the noise becoming overwhelming. To that point, these AirPods are actually FDA-certified hearing aids.

There are plenty of other features available here as well, especially if you have a compatible iPhone. AirPods Pro 3 have a built-in heart rate sensor, so you can track workouts without an Apple Watch; you can translate conversations in real time with Live Translate; "Conversation Awareness" lowers the volume of your audio and turns on transparency mode when you start speaking; and they run for eight hours on one charge with noise cancellation enabled.

This isn't an in-depth list of the AirPods Pro 3's set of features. But suffice it to say, these earbuds are worth their full MSRP of $249. So not only can I wholeheartedly recommend them at $149, but I'd say they're an easy buy if you've been thinking about picking up AirPods for yourself.

#3246. Apple Watch Series 12: Four standout features make me glad I upgraded

I upgraded to an Apple Watch Series 12 this fall (now $329 on Amazon), and there are four main features that make me especially glad I did.

The Apple Watch was overdue for a chip update, with Apple skipping any changes last year and not having any true performance upgrades since the S9.

I’m happy to report that the new S11 chip appears much faster and more capable than its predecessor, the S10.

Everyday tasks on Apple Watch Series 12 just feel fast. And Siri AI, a tentpole addition in watchOS 27, very much feels made for this latest hardware. Siri was sluggish on older hardware in my testing, but it performs much more like I’d hoped on Series 12.

The new Health Sensing System makes Apple Watch Series 12 better at tracking key metrics like heart rate and steps. But this isn’t a case where accuracy is the only improvement.

Because of the new health sensors, Series 12 offers three complications not available before:

The complications let you see up-to-date readings on your current heart rate, step count, and readiness score right from your watch face. These are very welcome additions that meaningfully improve the Apple Watch’s health and wellness feature set.

I’ve been using the watchOS 27.3 beta, which adds a new Siri Recap feature for Series 12 models that I really love.

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment.

Most of what Siri documents, I’ll never need to reference and it gets deleted automatically. But for those times I have trouble remembering a key piece of information, I’ve found Siri Recap a very convenient addition.

Apple Watch Series 12 offers largely the same battery life as Series 11, though it will last 25% longer for outdoor workouts.

More battery is always nice, but I’m especially a fan of the faster charging available on Series 12. Here’s how it stacks up to Series 11:

I wear my Apple Watch to bed and generally try to top it off quickly in the evening, but I’m not always great at giving it much time on the charger. With faster charging support on Series 12, my poor planning isn’t a problem.

Apple Watch Series 12 is now only $329 on Amazon, down from $399.

And because balance and strength decline and accelerate into your 50s, it's a crucial time for practicing yours. This one comes from a brilliant brand I use often, called Lifepro. I can tell you the quality of this product is excellent, with a grippy outer layer, a 10" Pilates ball, an inflation straw, a tape measure, and plugs. I train my dad on this every single week!

#3244. ‘Clashing Through The Snow’ Director Carlson Young Breaks Down Buc-ee’s Knockoff, Ryan’s Counsel From Chat GPT & Her Way Into The “Holiday Hijinks” Rom-Com

Clashing Through the Snow director Carlson Young found it easy to relate to the film’s two main characters, Ryan Mitchell (Christopher Briney) and Hannah Hendricks (Michelle Randolph).

The story centers the pair, two senior editors competing to oust the other from a condensed role due to impending layoffs, chasing big book deals for the publishing company where they work. Ryan operates off of commercial motivation and tapping into what is popular to sell books while Hannah identifies as more of a literary purist who takes big swings with the depth of books she takes on.

“[The script] really spoke to me. I felt so connected to Hannah and Ryan’s literary perspectives, and it felt like an existential conversation that I have with myself, moment to moment, constantly,” Young told Deadline. “It was easy for me to access their personalities and their inner worlds. And then I just loved the classic, holiday hijinks that ensue from there, and I was up for the challenge of trying to make a great holiday rom-com.” Watch on Deadline

The director connected the differing stances on what sells to challenges she navigates in her own job “balancing art and commerce, and what is and isn’t viable in storytelling and in the marketplace.”

RELATED: 7 New Christmas Movies Coming Out In 2026 From ‘Ebenezer’ To ‘Clashing Through The Snow’

“It is true that publishing and cinemas, these are tectonically shifting industries, and trying to find yourself your voice either as a book editor or director, whatever you’re doing, it doesn’t even need to be in a creative field,” she added. “But we’re all existing in these shifting sands, and so that was my way in. That’s why I was looking at it like that.”

In the below interview, Young unpacks specific moments like Lukas Gage’s “scene stealer” appearance, the Buc-ee’s knockoff Luc-ee’s, Ryan’s seeking advice by talking to ChatGPT and more.

DEADLINE: I spoke with Chris and Michelle earlier, and they mentioned you gave Chris a note comparing him to Jim Carrey. Did you have any other references? Could you expand on that?

CARLSON YOUNG: When we were rehearsing, I kept looking at him and seeing this physical comedy coming to the surface, and I was like, “This is like some Jim Carrey. I love this for you. Go off on that.” We tweaked it and trimmed it and shaped it in the edit, but he’s really funny. I hope that he does a lot more comedy.

DEADLINE: What was your role in the Luc-ee’s knockoff to Buc-ee’s?

YOUNG: I don’t know what I can and can’t say about Buc-ee’s/ Luc-ee’s, but we did our best. We did our version. I’m from Texas, Buc-ee’s is a big part of the psychology of a Texan, and so it was really funny, and we did our own version of it.

DEADLINE: For the part where Hannah’s in the helicopter venting to the pilot and Ryan’s driving the truck talking to AI, was there ever a plan to have him talking to a person or was it always going to be ChatGPT?

YOUNG: I have to say, yes, there was [a different iteration]. I personally thought that him talking to Chat was so Ryan. It made me laugh so much. And the amount of times that I’ve caught my husband… I’m like, ‘Are you asking ChatGPT a question? Like for real? Are you serious? ‘And he is serious. It just felt really modern and so of the times, and something like his character would actually do. And I like a lot the responses that Chat has for him. It just made me laugh.

DEADLINE: Lukas Gage is so funny in the small role he plays. He had a similar comedic presence in People We Meet on Vacation. How did you want to incorporate him in the storyline?

YOUNG: He’s a scene-stealer. You just give him an inch, and he will create a million miles of gold. He’s a spinster. And when we Facetimed about the character, he had the funniest ideas and instincts on it, like ‘He’s like Chris Elliott in Scary Movie.” I absolutely loved that. “That’s our north star. Let’s go do that.” He’s such a breath of fresh air once they get to the Mercyville Inn, and he’s such a phenomenal human. We’ll see him in, like, 100 more movies.

DEADLINE: Where did you shoot? Ryan and Hannah come from LA, but they get to New York on a road trip. How did you balance the different locations?

YOUNG: We shot in New York, a bit in the city, a bit upstate. We were shooting the Hudson Valley as you know Indiana and Colorado and Utah and it definitely lent itself. We were also experiencing historic winter weather in New York, like blizzards and production shut downs. Many a hurdle, and so it was truly ‘Clashing Through the Snow.’ We had a big snow budget, and we didn’t have to use it because it was just snow everywhere.

DEADLINE: Did the snow budget get redirected to other things?

YOUNG: Absolutely, girl. Our producers would have something to say about that.

DEADLINE: My mind goes to the music, which Prime Video is always good at getting, but the Olivia Rodrigo songs specifically…

YOUNG: That’s how we got the Olivia Rodrigo song. I like that story. I think we should go with that. We saved on snow, so we got this incredible Olivia Rodrigo song.

DEADLINE: Not only “Begged” in the film but “Take Me Home (4 Christmas)” was in the trailer.

YOUNG: I love her song in the film as well. We’re super lucky to have her.

DEADLINE: You’ve done Upgraded with Prime Video as well as The Last Sunrise. I know you’re not doing Upgraded 2, but is this a partnership you’re willing to continue, maybe in the form of The Last Sunrise sequel film when those books come out?

YOUNG: Absolutely, I could, definitely, and I just generally love working with this team at Amazon. They’re so collaborative and really cool people who have their finger on the pulse and they know what’s up. I feel like it’s such a creative environment that I love to work inside of. So yeah, ‘til the day I die, absolutely.
